In view of the fact that the throne speech made mention of amending certain legislation respecting veterans, and given the absolute desire on the part of Canada's veterans to have their own, sole minister of veterans affairs instead of presently having the Departments of Veterans Affairs and of National Defence downgraded to a dual ministry, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Lamontagne):
That the Prime Minister immediately pay proper respect to the veterans of Canada by appointing a minister whose specific responsibility will be the Department of Veterans Affairs, and at the same time give the members of Canada's Armed Forces their own full-time minister.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR CONTROLS ON INTEREST AND PROFIT MARGINS OF BANKS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that with every increase in the Bank of Canada's interest rate, the chartered banks use this opportunity to increase the margin between what they pay depositors and what they charge borrowers, and in view of the fact that these same banks in the third quarter of this year were paying taxes at a rate of just over 10 per cent on ever-spiralling profits, thus increasing the burden on the working taxpayer, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House call for immediate controls on interest and profit margins in the banking industry, and the imposition of a surtax on the banks to bring their effective tax rate to 50 per cent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of the utmost urgency.
Given the plight of the six Polish sailors who have jumped ship in St. John's, Newfoundland, in the hope of being granted refugee status in Canada so as to escape the burden of oppressive dictatorship in their native Poland, and given the fact that this matter was brought to the attention of both the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) more than two weeks ago, with no action having been taken, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan):
That this House call upon the minister of immigration to exercise his ministerial prerogative and immediately issue permission for these sailors to remain in Canada.

speechtext:

In view of the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) has unilaterally cut off Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba from Canada Works funding, including many regions like the Churchill constituency which has areas of unemployment exceeding 80 per cent, and has justified his actions by counting only the number of UIC beneficiaries rather than the number of unemployed people to determine the qualifying rate, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the risk of repeating myself, I would like again to add my name to those who have congratulated the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) on the manner in which they moved and seconded the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I would also like to preface my remarks by stating my sincere appreciation to the people of Ottawa Centre for the confidence they demonstrated in me on May 22. Ottawa Centre is indeed a unique riding, and I am honoured to represent its electors. The Parliament Buildings are located within its boundary thereby creating a federal presence known nowhere else in Canada, as I mentioned last night.
There is another dimension which I believe is characteristic of few other ridings. Ottawa Centre is, in my mind, a microcosm of the country itself. It has a wide range of cultural, social, economic and political groups making it a true reflection of the vertical mosaic which is Canada, a mosaic in which each individual contributes in his or her own unique way to the strength and vitality of Canadian society.
The people of Ottawa Centre also represent a group of Canadians who I believe are better informed than their peers on matters of public policy and their implications. They feel the intimate presence of four levels of government and have demonstrated their ability to voice reasoned opinions on the issues of the day.
However, while the pervasive federal presence has certain advantages for Ottawans, there are also very real disadvantages. The advantages are, of course, the many amenities which accompany the physical location of the seat of government. The Parliament Buildings, the National Arts Centre, the Museum of Man, the canal, the National Art Gallery, the Supreme Court, the National Library, the Garden of the Provinces, the Postal Museum and the Bank of Canada are all located in the riding of Ottawa Centre and are a source of pride and enjoyment for the people of Ottawa Centre and, indeed, for all Canadians who take the opportunity to visit our truly beautiful city.
October 12, 1979

Much credit should be given to the National Capital Commission which has played, and continues to play, a vital role in the beautification and maintenance of the region. However, the actions of the National Capital Commission have also created in the past problems arising as a result of the commission's taking decisions without fully involving the citizens who are affected. To overcome this problem, Mr. Speaker, I urge the government to direct the National Capital Commission to establish an effective consultation mechanism and to take essential decisions on land use or other matters only after full and extensive consultations have taken place with the municipal and regional governments.
I also urge the government to follow the lead of the former minister of finance and to bring forward much needed amendments to the Municipal Grants Act. This is a matter of great concern to the municipalities in the National Capital Region, as well as to municipalities across Canada where there is a federal presence. However, the inadequacy of current grants in lieu of taxes is of paramount importance here in Ottawa due to the degree to which the federal government permeates our lives. Ottawa is heavily dependent on these grants for operating revenues, and local property taxes, which are among the highest in Canada, reflect the extent to which the federal government has failed to pay its fair share. Let me again urge the government to move expeditiously on this matter in order to alleviate the unfair financial burden which has fallen on the citizens of Ottawa.
Turning to another point, one of the main concerns of the constituents of Ottawa Centre is the government's intention to cut the public service by 60,000 jobs over the next three years. This is a part of the government's austerity program, and I cannot emphasize strongly enough the need to approach this matter carefully. This action by the government will not only affect public servants in Ottawa but those across the country. My riding in particular will be hard hit due to its large percentage of public servants. This, in turn, will have a spillover effect on the private sector in Ottawa. The small businesses in my riding are heavily dependent on the purchasing power of public servants as well as on services obtained by the government on a contractual basis. The unemployment figures in Ottawa will, without question, rise significantly under this policy and it will take years for the city to recover its present financial base.
The people affected, some of whom have been in the employ of the federal government for decades, will never recover. We are talking about people; they are not merely numbers to be thrown around at the whim of the government. These are people who have dedicated their lives to providing valuable services to their fellow Canadians, and this is hardly the thanks they deserve. The citizens of Ottawa Centre, my constituents, represent the backbone of the federal public service. It is the responsibility of the government to ensure that their efforts are recognized and that they receive fair and equitable treatment. This is not accomplished by perpetuating uncertainty about their employment future nor by implementing poorly conceived policies in the name of restraint.
The Address-Mr. Evans
The lack of certainty about job security is having a very real negative impact on all public servants and certainly is affecting the quality of service provided to the public. The prospect of unemployment during these difficult times is serious indeed.
In the Speech from the Throne, the government indicated its intention to bring forward special measures to assist youth, women and native Canadians. I urge this government to expand these measures to include assistance to the public servants who will be affected by these reductions and who will require retraining to ensure continuing employment opportunities. It is the very least they can do for those who have proven their loyalty and their commitment to the federal government and the people of Canada.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) has met with all local area members of parliament as well as with the representatives of the cities of Ottawa and Hull, the regional municipalities of Ottawa-Carleton and the Outaouais and the local business community. At this meeting, the minister publicly acknowledged the adverse effects which the government's restraint program would have on the region and on public servants. He also stated that a compensation program would be established to offset these effects. Further, he agreed to form a task force to identify problems being encountered by the business community and to aid in preparing a plan of economic diversification for the region.
This task force was to have been established by the end of September. To date, we have heard nothing further from the President of the Treasury Board. I wish to remind him of his commitment to the people and local governments of the region. He must assume his responsibilities immediately. He must establish the promised task force and he must clearly define the nature of the financial assistance he is prepared to grant to affected communities and their citizens. To this end, Mr. Speaker, I call upon the President of the Treasury Board to act now. I also urge the President of the Treasury Board to reintroduce the equivalent of Bill C-12, which was introduced in the last session, dealing with public service pensions. This would provide a safeguard for indexed public service pensions and an opportunity to examine the feasibility of the indexing of pensions in the private sector.
The question of public servant involvement in the political process is also a matter of concern to my constituents. It is my strong belief that public servants should be entitled to the same rights as other Canadians and should be permitted to support and work for the party of their choice. This would involve amending the Public Service Employment Act, and I call upon the government to do so at the earliest possible opportunity.
I listened with anticipation to the Speech from the Throne for new things to come for Canada, for the promised "new directions" in economic policy which would bring forth growth and development. While I was heartened by the promises of an early introduction of freedom of information legislation and reforms to improve the efficiency of Parliament, I was totally disappointed in the lack of direction shown by the government in the economic area. After 16 years as the official opposition

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. Evans
and four and one half months as government, it would seem reasonable to expect a clear definition of the economic policies which the government intends to employ in leading us to the "promised land".
However, what was said indicates without a doubt that there is no new economic policy to be introduced and no economic leadership on the horizon. The government appears to be experiencing technical difficulty in forming any clear ideas, as witnessed by their reluctance to bring down a new budget. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) indicates that the earliest he could bring down a budget is at least a month away, which will mean the government will have been six full months in power. This is a sad commentary for a party which when in opposition boasted of having all the answers.
The global community is experiencing hard times, Mr. Speaker, and Canada is no exception. Canada needs specific policies, not the vague generalities presented so far by the government, policies which will provide the leadership necessary to ensure that the 1980s is a period of economic growth and prosperity.
Canada needs specific policies today, Mr. Speaker, not in months or years after endless study and consultation. The government has decided that, rather than explore new ideas and give priority to the economy, it is far more beneficial to spend its time undoing what has already been done in the interest of all Canadians. Examples of that to which I allude are Loto Canada, Petro-Canada and offshore mineral and petroleum rights. In all cases, the government's actions represent, to my mind, a total disregard of the rights of all Canadians in an attempt to placate the provinces. This is closely related to the stated promise of provincial status for the Yukon. Does this mean the tiny population of 23,000 people will be given full ownership and control of the vast resources of the Yukon, resources which up to now have belonged to all Canadians? If so, Mr. Speaker, it is the greatest sell-out of all time and a total derogation of the government's responsibility to the nation.
Mr. Speaker, this government does not appear to have a vision of Canada as a unified whole; rather it sees Canada as a conglomerate of fractional parts. In the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, this government raises serious questions as to its grasp of the dynamics of nationhood, how, in fact, all parts of the country should strive to work together in harmony, to achieve its collective as well as individual goals.
I sense a growing uneasiness, Mr. Speaker, among Canadians over the apparent lack of concern by the central government for the interests of Canada. Its concern seems to be for the parts rather than for the unified whole. Mr. Speaker, I feel that this dangerous lack of national perspective is leading to policy formulation which will seriously hinder the ability of the central government to speak effectively for all Canadians.
I am in full support of consensus rather than confrontation when such consensus is possible and consistent with the national interest. As an example, Mr. Speaker, I will draw upon
[Mr. Evans.)
energy policy. This is a matter which touches all Canadians. It is a case of such pressing importance that whether or not consensus can be reached with the provinces, the federal government must, as the representative of all Canadians, take action. With this government, Mr. Speaker, I have yet to see any indication of a willingness to take such action, even though it is becoming abundantly clear that a consensus is likely to be impossible to achieve. Indeed, it may not be possible to reach any multilateral solution.
Mr. Speaker, there is a train of thought which appears to permeate the Speech from the Throne: that is, a lack of confidence by this government in themselves and in their fellow parliamentarians' abilities to represent the needs of their constituents. As members of parliament, we represent ridings from all regions. Our role is to represent the interests of our electors within a national context. These same electors vote for representatives in the provincial legislatures to represent their interests falling under provincial jurisdiction. It puzzles me that this government appears to have come to the conclusion that provincial representatives and premiers can better appreciate and serve the needs of Canadians than can federal representatives and the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), even in areas of federal jurisdiction.
Under this illusion, the government is apparently prepared to extend rights to the provinces which will undermine the effectiveness of the federal government and reduce the mandate given to it by the Canadian electorate. Mr. Speaker, I totally reject the notion of decentralized power when it will compromise the work being done by Parliament on behalf of all Canadians.
Another point which indicates the undoing philosophy of this government, Mr. Speaker, is found in a recent speech given by the minister of social programs. He indicated the new direction the government is planning to take with regard to pensions. He said and I quote, "We will be placing more emphasis on selectivity than on universality". Mr. Speaker, this raises a whole host of questions and demonstrates a naive view of the operation of social programs. Does he realize, Mr. Speaker, that it is often less costly to run a universal program than a selective one, due to the substantial cost of administration, monitoring and policing? Apparently not, since no mention of these considerations was made in his speech.
My estimation is that in the case of pensions, a regulatory body would have to be established which would all but eliminate any potential savings, not to mention the invasion of privacy which would result from monitoring and the concern which would be caused senior citizens. These are who are having a difficult time now and who may be short-changed with the introduction of a new system. Senior citizens must be assured financial security. I have already heard from many senior citizens in my riding on this matter. Their concern is great, and they are extremely worried about their future under this government. Mr. Speaker, to harass the elderly with such off-the-cuff statements is not only irresponsible but cruel. Our senior citizens have given the best years of their lives to the building of this country. All they ask is basic financial security
October 12, 1979

in their retirement years. Mr. Speaker, I implore the government to rethink this whole matter.
1 also call upon this new government to bring forward legislation in the competition field, especially as it relates to corporate mergers. Canada must have effective competition law, especially in view of the heavy private sector emphasis of this government.
The lack of a clear policy on energy in the Speech from the Throne is of deep concern to me. With the inevitability of rising energy prices the serious question of transfers of wealth and their implications for the economy comes to the fore. How does the government intend to offset increased prices for low income groups and small businesses whose expenses are often dependent on the price of oil, and how will they ensure the availability of renewable substitutes? Mr. Speaker, it is hoped the government will in fact take an aggressive stance with regard to research and development in the energy field, a stance which will not rely totally on the private sector, which has lacked the motivation in the past.
My final point, Mr. Speaker, relates to language training for newcomers to Canada. This has become a matter of some concern to me. A large number of my constituents speak neither English nor French. It is my belief that the government of Canada has a responsibility to such newcomers; a responsibility to ensure that adequate facilities and training are available to allow their learning of one or the other official language. Language training is essential if people new to Canada are to feel at home in their new country and are to participate fully in Canadian life. 1 call upon the government to review the situation and to bring forward policies to resolve the problem.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to state again what an honour it is to represent the people of Ottawa Centre in this House. Ottawa Centre has had a tradition of good, solid and effective representation and 1 intend to do my very best to maintain that tradition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate you on your selection as Deputy Speaker and compliment you on the work you have done in the past. I am sure it will be of a comparable standard in the future.
I should also like to compliment the mover and seconder of the motion in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I have heard several of these speeches and I feel their calibre and their recognition of the significance of their position deserves special mention. When they read the records of this House I am sure they will read what they have said with pride compared to maiden speeches by other members of the House with the same responsibility. Their constituents have every right to be proud of the manner in which they conducted themselves.
One of the things which seems to be typical of this House at the moment, Mr. Speaker, is an assumption by those on your left that there is absolutely no problem in the government placing itself in a firm position; that every minister should have every policy in place and ready to proceed; that every-
The Address-Mr. McCain
thing should be running exactly as members opnosite think it should, as if no change had ever taken place and as if it were not necessary to become acquainted with new responsibilities. Of course, such is not the case. I believe that exploiting the problems of the short period the government has been in office does not do credit to those who make such comments.
Let me give you an example, Mr. Speaker, of the complete lack of attention to important affairs which was exhibited by the former government. Perhaps those who criticize will then show more consideration if everything does not happen exactly at the moment they think it should.
During the summer, members of the government were plagued with problems. Backbench members of the government were the communicators of these problems to the responsible ministers. My first problem arose from the fact that in my constituency there is a laboratory structure, Huntsman Marine Laboratories of St. Andrews, which is not an arm of the government but which does operate in fisheries research as a contract agent for the Government of Canada.
In December, 1978, after long negotiations, it was agreed by the then minister of fisheries, by the Huntsman Marine Laboratories and by the research branch of the department of fisheries that the Huntsman Marine group should go forward with their experimentation in salmon, particularly genetic research. This research included trying to trace down where salmon will best propagate, where it will best spend its summers, how it winters in the sea, how we can get salmon to return to its spawning grounds, and to find out what are the hardiest and healthiest species of salmon that we can develop. In May this group had not been assured that money was available and were having to go to the bank to borrow money.
Bear in mind that this contract was completed in every detail in December. It was approved by the minister of fisheries. In June I received a call from the director of that branch and he said, "We have not received any money from Ottawa." He told me they had had to go to the bank to borrow money because the money was not voted by the government prior to the election call. The money may have been in the budget, but what had not happened was that necessary applications had not been made to the Treasury Board. Therefore, the actual expenditure was never authorized by the government for a contract negotiated in December, and the government went out of office on May 22.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) before he starts his speech, but I had overlooked earlier today resolving a point of order that had been raised yesterday by the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen). I was reminded of it and I thought I should try at this moment to regulate it because the House, I believe, depends on some resolution of the problem in terms of future business, perhaps even later this day.
The point of order raised concerned the tabling yesterday of the spending estimates by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) and the absence of having a declaration by the President of the Treasury Board that he recommended the estimates to the House. The estimates carried with them the usual recommendation from His Excellency but no statement was made by the President of the Treasury Board upon the tabling of the estimates.
When the point was raised yesterday, there was participation in the discussion by the President of the Treasury Board
October 12, 1979

who indicated that he was confirming his action specifically. His action was an intentional one of tabling the estimates and taking no further action.
During the course of the discussion, one of the participants was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who suggested something that would have been somewhat an inevitable course in any research of the matter, that is to examine what had been done by previous finance ministers. From research going back 20 years, I can report to the House that on several occasions, in fact on most occasions, a statement was made by the minister of finance on the tabling of the estimates. That is to say, during the tabling of documents, the estimates have been tabled by the President of the Treasury Board and then followed by a statement.
Under our present practices, upon the calling of "Statements by Ministers", a statement was made by the minister which had some explanatory effect in respect of the estimates. However, I am not able to discover in any of those that those statements contained the recommendation of the President of the Treasury Board that these estimates be accepted by the House, certainly not in a formal way. While that may have been inferred from some of the statements, it was not done in a formal way.
Furthermore, and I am going from memory here, I believe that upon the change of government in 1957, the President of the Treasury Board or whoever was acting at that time, on the tabling of the estimates, did precisely the same as was done yesterday by the President of the Treasury Board. I can be more specific here. It was the Hon. Donald M. Fleming, then minister of finance, who, as reported on Tuesday, October 15, 1957, took precisely the action that was taken yesterday on tabling the estimates, taking no further action.
Whatever arguments that may lead to in terms of discussion or debate, of course, remains open. I only have the responsibility to deal with the point of order as to whether it is a requirement and an essential part of Parliament and its practices and parliamentary responsibility for the finance minister or the President of the Treasury Board, upon the tabling of estimates, to indicate at that time in a specific declaration that he asks for the approval of the House of those estimates. I cannot find any authority for that proposition. Therefore, in regulating the narrow point of order which was raised yesterday, I have to set it aside.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept fully everything that you have said. There is no difference at all between us. I believe the situation that developed yesterday is quite different from any situation to which you have alluded, namely that we had a message from His Excellency recommending the estimates to the House. The simple point is that I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) whether he recommended these estimates to the House and he would not tell us. That puts in doubt whether the message of His Excellency in recommending the estimates to the House carries with it the advice of his ministers. That is all.
Privilege-Mr. MacEachen
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) missed the point also, because the point arose when the question was asked and no answer was given. Today we do not know from any member of the government whether this message came from Government House, as it were from His Excellency, without the advice and recommendation of the ministry.
I have raised that question and I am asking why it is that yesterday the President of the Treasury Board would not say that they were recommending the estimates to the House. Are they or are they not, or is His Excellency acting on his own? That is the only point.
The position is as clear as crystal in Erskine May, which says that the Crown, acting with the advice of its responsible ministers, makes known to the Commons the pecuniary necessities of the government. Yesterday the Crown made known the pecuniary necessities, but we have not yet been told, and it arose when the question was asked, whether he was acting with the advice of his ministers. If he is, of course, it means that the ministry is recommending these estimates to the House.
May I say that I am not going to pursue it procedurally and ask Your Honour to do anything further, but I intend to pursue it at a later stage when it comes to putting the estimates to committee, because we do not intend to accept any procedure until we know whether the government is recommending these estimates to the House.
I accept fully what you have said, Mr. Speaker, but I must say respectfully that it does not deal with the political question that I raised of how the House can receive estimates until it knows whether they are recommended by the responsible ministers.
Nit-picking.

October 12, 1979
Privilege-Mr. MacEachen
Are we now in the position of having to obtain the consent of the House in order to move that motion, because it might be appropriate if we did move the motion to send the estimates now tabled to the appropriate standing committees. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to give consent the moment the ministry accepts its constitutional responsibility and tells the House it is recommending the estimates to the House, and that it put the words in the mouth of His Excellency that this House take the estimates and pass them. If that is done we will be very co-operative.

Mr. Speaker, we, too, are quite prepared to give consent to the making of the motion to refer the estimates to the standing committees provided the condition to which Your Honour has referred has been met, namely, that the committees have been established.
I understand that the report from the striking committee is ready-obviously I understand that because I am a member of the striking committee. If that report can be made some time this day and approved, then the estimates could be referred to the various committees. Perhaps that could be done at two o'clock or at five o'clock or at some time today and we would give the required consent.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I feel I must say a word about some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen). We are often on the same wave length, but whatever wave length he is on today I think he is drawing an awfully long bow. After all, if it were true that His Excellency the Governor General, without the approval of the government of the day, was recommending estimates to this House, we would have a constitutional revolution on our hands. The Governor General whose capacities some of us know quite well, has no way of communicating a message to this House except through a minister.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) has tabled the estimates and has given with them a message from His Excellency the Governor General approving those estimates. That surely implies that the President of the Treasury

Board or somebody else in the government asked the Governor General to do so. He could not do it on his own.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sinclair Stevens (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I shall be able to clarify this matter. With all due respect to the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen), I felt he was being overly technical when this point was raised yesterday. I was relying on a ruling by yourself, Mr. Speaker, on February 18, 1976, when the then president of treasury board, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), in the process of doing precisely what I was doing yesterday, namely, tabling estimates, went on to elaborate on the tabling. Your Honour interrupted him and said:
Order, please. I feel the hon. President of Treasury Board is making a statement as a minister and this calls for an answer from representatives of all political parties in the House. In addition, there will be a question later. If such is the minister's intention I urge him to continue. If not, we shall have to remain at the document-tabling stage.
Your Honour went on to say:
I have an indication, now, from the minister that it is not his intention to make a statement at this time but simply to table the document.
That is not the issue!

Yesterday when I was asked whether I recommended the estimates I felt I did not wish to make a statement and had no further comment other than to say 1 had tabled the main estimates.
If I might deal now with the point which has been reiterated, I would draw Your Honour's attention to Standing Order 62(1) which requires that the House not deal with supply matters without the proposal first being recommended by the Governor General. This indicates that the President of Treasury Board must transmit the message from the Governor General to the Speaker to be read to the House, which I did yesterday. There is absolutely no indication, constitutional or otherwise, that we have to recommend the estimates or make any comment at that stage.
Perhaps I might briefly outline the process. I might add I am very surprised that the hon. member, with his long experience, is not aware of it. I did sign the letter to His Excellency the Governor General in Council in which I said:
The undersigned has the honour to submit to His Excellency the Governor General in Council the estimates of sums required for the service of Canada for the year ending on the thirty-first of March, 1980. and advises that His Excellency may be pleased to recommend these estimates to the House of Commons in accordance with the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867.
Respectfully submitted
That letter was signed by myself and I am willing to table it. In due course the Governor General did respond with the message which I transmitted to Your Honour yesterday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The matter is now fully resolved. The question of consent both to the reception of the report of the striking committee and then, in turn, to the motion to send these estimates to the committees will have to be dealt with by consent on returning to those separate aspects of our routine
October 12, 1979

proceedings, which consent I am sure the House will facilitate at the appropriate time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All I say is this, Mr. Speaker. If the minister would say to the House what he has said to the Governor General, namely, that he recommends the estimates to the House, we would be happy to give consent now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
Let me come briefly to the subject matter 1 was touching on before, the difficulties of the takeover and the delays which sometimes occurred. The instance which I have already cited can again be exemplified by three others, one at the port of Saint John, and another with respect to the dredging of the Miramichi.
The Address-Mr. McCain
It is the habit of government to say, "Yes, we will do a job". Having said that the job will be done, the final proof that it will be done is when the order of the Treasury Board which actually authorizes the expenditure of the money for the particular project has been passed. That money was not authorized for the port development in Saint John, nor was it completely authorized for an expenditure by the Treasury Board for the dredging of the Miramichi. I would like to draw to the attention of the people of New Brunswick that while a promise of a government had been made, it could only be kept by the actual authorization of expenditure and approval of that expenditure by the Treasury Board. This was not done, yet the people of New Brunswick are under the impression that the money indeed had been authorized, and it should indeed be.
There are a number of problems in Atlantic Canada. I was very interested in listening to the hon. member for Humber-Port-Au-Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Faour) yesterday when he suggested that Petro-Canada should take over the refinery at Come-by-Chance. I think that can only be considered in light of the fact that in the six eastern provinces of Canada there exists today a refining capability of 750,000 barrels in excess of Canada's consuming capability.
If Petro-Canada were to assume responsibility for Come-by-Chance at this moment in time, where is the market to be found? I submit that one of the objectives any government of Canada should have had historically and must have in the future is to arrange for transfer of some energy between Canada and the United States, including the transfer of that energy which can be refined in that excessive refining capacity which exists in eastern Canada. Then and only then can Come-by-Chance become viable for Petro-Canada or any company.
I might say in passing that one of my concerns about Crown corporations in any sphere is that public and political pressures to take on non-viable operations may very well strangle Crown corporations. They may very well get into the heavily debt-ridden position experienced by the CNR. It may be necessary down the road, if we succumb to the political pressures expressed in this House, for a corporation such as Petro-Canada to have to rely on taxpayers to bail it out as we bailed CNR out last year and as we bailed it out on two earlier occasions to the extent of something in excess of $2 billion in total. I think this is the result of political pressures to have Crown corporations meet political needs. This is not the way to serve the nation effectively and efficiently.
The agricultural industry of Canada has experienced a great many difficulties. One part of that industry which is experiencing a very serious difficulty at the moment is the potato industry, which has over-produced on a national basis, according to Statistics Canada, and which may be deprived of a part of its export markets by virtue of a decision made by some authority in the European Economic Community. That decision was that Canada should not ship seed potatoes to Italy from this crop year's production. This has been a market which has been taking an increasing quantity of seed potatoes

October 12, 1979
The Address

Mr. McCain
from Atlantic Canada, and if this market is denied us for phyto-sanitary reasons, that will simply add to the surplus which must be disposed of in Canada.
I implore the Government of Canada to use every possible effort to get a renewal of the privilege to export seed potatoes to Italy this year and also to undertake ongoing negotiations to get a long-term and not an annual permit for their shipment. This decision has a very serious impact upon Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick production, but it also has an impact on Ontario, Quebec and perhaps even Manitoba production because what does not leave the shore as seed will most certainly have to be marketed as table stock or dumped.
This is a very unfortunate picture, but it is precisely the way it is. I understand that there are ongoing negotiations, that Italy is making the strongest possible political representations to the European Economic Community to have it accept Canadian seed potatoes into that market, and that there will be a meeting within the next ten days to two weeks between the trade officials of this country and the community. Along with the influence and the expertise of the Department of Agriculture, I hope that the trade representatives of Canada will be able to get the concession needed to ship seed potatoes to Europe.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
The minister is a very competent guy. I would be happy to entrust the potato industry into his hands. I hope he will have time, and if it becomes that serious, I am sure he will go.
The plight of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada is rather serious in many ways. As a result of over-exploitation and a failure to supervise the catch of many species in adjacent waters to our shores, the population was depleted to the point that it was very difficult to make a livelihood. It became necessary to impose catch and licensing restrictions upon the industry. These licensing restrictions have been carried to excess. As the stock is replacing itself as a result of more controlled catch, I believe the time has now come when licences must be issued to more fishermen.
I want to compliment the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) on his remarks yesterday in the House. There is no man in the House who has as practical a knowledge of the fishing industry as the hon. member for South Shore. He epitomized that in his remarks-his expression of interest and his pursuit of a more generous treatment by the Department of Fisheries of the fishing industry.
How serious is this situation? In the last ten years the cost of boat replacement has risen threefold. That is out of all proportion to the inflation rate affecting Canada in general. The cost of gear and equipment has risen an equal amount or more. On top of those factors, today the fisherman is faced with an interest rate-and has been for the past two years- which, if he must finance the boat by means other than his own catch, pyramids the cost of that boat by another one, two

or threefold depending upon the terms of the financing. Then it becomes a very expensive operation. Coupled with that is the fact that young people are not allowed to get licences because there are restrictions and limitations upon those who can be licensed. Also there is a restriction upon the transfer of the licence from an older fisherman to a younger one.
These restrictions must be re-examined. As we have attempted to keep young people on the farms, there must be some way to attempt to keep young people in the fishing industry. But under the regulations which we inherited, this is virtually impossible. If we are to replace the existing generation of fishermen, there must be a relaxation of the licensing procedures. In view of the tremendous increase in the cost of boats and equipment, it is imperative that some kind of reasonable financial operation be set up to make it possible for fishermen to buy boats and make the necessary payment arrangements without interest as burdesome as it is in the open market.
As I have suggested many times in the House, we must have a Central Mortgage and Housing or a Farm Credit Corporation-type of lending agency in government which will permit young fishermen, and even some of the older ones, to obtain short-term financing for the improvement and replacement of their equipment and boats. I beseech the government to give this serious consideration in its future deliberations.
There is a particular problem in my constituency respecting transportation. The commitments of confederation were that products in any part of Canada should have transportation costs which would permit that part of Canada to trade with the rest of Canada. Recently freight rate increases on the roads and by rail have risen to the point where many commodities are no longer competitive in what were the historic markets in Canada when rail rates were at a different level. This requires serious examination as does the transportation of wheat. On a smaller scale it is as vital to the Atlantic economy as is the transportation of wheat to the western economy.
Earlier it was said in the House that if there is a weak section in Canada economically, it weakens all of Canada. As long as transportation costs remain at the present level, or as long as by international trade agreements we have to trade within Canada and not overseas or with the neighbouring country to the south on a basis which would be competitive with them, then we must have transportation structures and costs to allow us to resume the trade which was historically ours in this nation.
In particular I should like to refer to the ferry service which runs from the mainland of New Brunswick to the Island of Grand Manan. Historically the Government of Canada assumed quite a large responsibility for ferries operating in salt water. Except in the St. Lawrence and in one or two of the Great Lakes areas, it did not assume any financial responsibility for ferry services required in fresh water. Some years ago an agreement was signed between the Government of Canada and New Brunswick that the Grand Manan ferry would be subsidized to the extent of $150,000 by the province of New Brunswick, in round figures, and $267,000 by the federal
October 12, 1979

government. But there was no clause for indexing the cost of the federal subsidy. As inflation has stormed down on us, the cost of operating that ferry has risen immensely. Since there was no indexing in the federal subsidy, there has been no increment in the payment to the province of New Brunswick. The province of New Brunswick will find itself in a position this year where it will probably pay $1,600,000 as subsidy. That is a tenfold increase from the original $150,000 subsidy, partly as a result of inflation and partly as a result of an increase in Grand Manan fishing and its fish processing industry.
This matter must be reconsidered. I will not take the time of the House to go into all the details, but if the Department of Transport will examine its records it will find that subsidies are paid for comparable ferries in other Canadian provinces in a much more generous fashion. That much more generous fashion should be applied to this particular ferry. When one looks at CN Marine, one will find that not only have we assisted by tax dollars the operation of ferries in Canada, but also the operation of an international ferry on the Bay of Fundy. I submit Grand Manan should come first; the province of New Brunswick should come first. The burden of financing this service certainly should be assumed to a greater extent by the Government of Canada.
There has been a great deal of discussion about the maritime energy commission. It was a proposal by the former government based on the philosophy that certain gains could be obtained by co-operation on the part of the commission and the maritime provinces. Initially it was hoped that it would be the Atlantic provinces, but that was not going to work out. 1 urge the government of Canada to take a very long and hard look at the possibilities of developing electrical energy in the maritime provinces. It is absolutely imperative that every Atlantic province seek the lowest possible cost of energy.
The Government of Canada has in the past seen fit to extend the credit rating of the Government of Canada to developments in Canada without subsidizing them, but by merely guaranteeing a loan or by borrowing and lending the money to the operation in Canada. This happened initially with the Beechwood dam on the Saint John River and resulted in a very extensive saving for the province of New Brunswick without costing the Government of Canada a dime.
It is from this base that the Government of Canada should commit itself, not necessarily to gifts to Atlantic Canada, which is not what I am asking and not what I am proposing. I am proposing that it would be propitious for the Government of Canada to guarantee to the maritime energy commission the loans it would have to float in order to build the projects which are available.
One of the things which I think might very well be profitable to Canada, and particularly to the maritimes, at this moment in time is the construction of enough generating capability that some of this energy could be exported to the United States eastern seaboard. I propose this because I
The Address-Mr. McCain
believe there is a market there and a fair profit to be obtained from this, a profit which might very well make a major contribution to the reduction in energy costs both for the New England seaboard and for the maritime provinces. I think we should take a look at this as a business proposition.
I have heard members of this House and people in New Brunswick scream about the idea that we would export electric energy or that we would build in excess of immediate demand, but in every instance where this has happened, and it has in three or four instances in New Brunswick, the exporting of energy has in the long run contributed to a lower cost supply of energy for New Brunswick.
I believe it is along this course that the Government of Canada should move in a serious way with negotiations for the establishment of the maritime energy commission, and that it should plead with the premiers of the maritime provinces to sit down around the same table in order to arrive at a common goal, and thus save money both for Canada and for the provinces.
The forest industry in eastern Canada to a greater degree than in the rest of Canada, but also the forest industry in all of Canada, has had a very heavy withdrawal of capital resources by cutting, which has been excessive in some areas. Coupled with this it has had an insect and bacterial infestation which is reducing the live and useful wood in this country. I plead with the minister responsible for forestry and the minister responsible for the environment to act in consultation particularly with the province of New Brunswick, which has had no choice but to spray, and to arrive at the best possible scientific way to control the infestation which is depleting our forest resources in Canada. This is a matter for research and it may be a matter for financing.
There has been circulated to all members of the House of Commons a very definite and detailed picture of the depletion of this industry, showing the necessity for protection from fire and pests and the necessity for reforestation. In view of the fact that it is our largest single employer and our largest single exporter, and in view of the fact that it is one of our largest taxpayers, paying directly or indirectly to the Government of Canada almost a billion dollars, and paying to the municipalities and the provinces of Canada more than a billion dollars in taxes, it is a vital aspect of our economic picture, both to the workers in the field and to their representatives in the House of Commons.
An industry of this magnitude must receive more attention and more consideration by the Government of Canada than it has in the past. I have been encouraged by the remarks I have heard to date from this government, and somewhat discouraged by some of those I have been accustomed to hearing over the past few years.
I will not bore the House any longer, Mr. Speaker, with the needs of my constituency or with things I feel the government should do. I very much thank the opposition whip for his tolerance and I assure him that I will respect the recommendation he made earlier in the day.

October 12, 1979
The Address-Miss Jewett

On a
personal note, Mr. Speaker, may I say what a pleasure it is to be back in this House. It is a particular pleasure to be here as a British Columbian and as a member of the NDP, and to follow my distinguished predecessor, Stuart Lcggatt, in both respects.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
1 had not yet seen the light in either respect when I was here before, although on looking again at my first speech given in May, 1963, I thought how close it came to the NDP position on almost all matters. Of course, those were the days of relatively enlightened Liberalism, days long since past as the events of last evening once again showed.
That first speech of mine was also made during a throne speech debate. Like the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), I moved the address in reply. I hope I acquitted myself as well as he and the seconder, the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald), did the other day. Not that they had much to work with. They were robbed of guidance in many fields, those relating to the economy, the constitution, the Quebec referendum and the entire field of international affairs, and it is the latter I want to say a few words about, first, this afternoon.
1 believe there has been no occasion, certainly in my memory, when international affairs has not been mentioned in a Speech from the Throne. Not only was this subject not mentioned in this Speech from the Throne, it was not mentioned at all in the address of the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). As I say, surely this is the first time in a very long while that this has happened.
It may well be that the difficulties the government got into by making too early, too premature and too unthought-out pronouncements, particularly in the matter of moving the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, caused it to shy away completely from the whole field of Canada in the world today. Surely this cannot be because the government does not know that Canada has a position. Members of the government talked about this, not so much during the election campaign but on many occasions during the last Parliament. It must be because of the premature move they made and to which once again today in question period they could not either say, Look, it was a mistake. We do not intend to move the embassy ', or "Yes, we have this ambassador looking at everything, but as I, the Prime Minister, remarked right after the election, it is only the timing of the move that is in question". Surely the government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald), who did her best to help the Prime Minister on an earlier occasion, could have said one or the other.
This government wants very much to restore confidence. It wants very much to restore the faith of the private sector in which it very strongly believes, in the Government of Canada and in Canada itself. How can it restore that faith when it does not make clear to business concerns what its position in

relation to the move of the embassy is. It should not be made some time down the road, but now. The government's lack of position, obviously, is creating uncertainty. The answers of the minister and of the Prime Minister this morning, although they may have been further amplified at a press conference since then, have not been satisfactory.
The other reason why the government made no mention of international affairs must be that the government does not know, particularly in the fields of aid and perhaps I should also mention peacekeeping-two of the cornerstones of foreign policy in the past years-in what direction it wishes to go. There are conflicting signals. In her speech at the United Nations, my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who I know would have been here this afternoon because I told her I would be speaking but has been otherwise engaged, said that Canada was still concerned about the human rights of all people; that the human rights of all people were what mattered more than anything else; that specifically as we look into the decades before us, it is the countries at the bottom end of the economic scale which face the bleakest future and the lowest growth.
I believe she spoke at that time in her compassionate, humanitarian, progressive spirit about the problems of the poorer nations and the need for respect for human rights everywhere. That was expressed in the minister's speech at the United Nations. A few weeks later in a speech to the Empire Club, the minister did a complete turn-around. She then suggested that it was not the poorer nations that needed our continued compassion and concern, but it was those nations on the brink of development which were breaking through and which would soon become established as strong economic units. She suggested that we had not been taking into sufficient account the economic returns which Canada could expect in both the short and the long term. She suggested that we should also look very closely at our political and economic relations before we decided with particular countries whether aid should be extended.
The minister said in her speech at the Empire Club:
Is it really the right thing to do, to divorce aid policy entirely from the rest of our relations, both political and economic, with the country concerned.
In the speech which the minister gave a few weeks before at the United Nations she said:
There is growing recognition that development assistance does not imply the foisting of one country's economic and social philosophy on another.
What had caused the change in the intervening weeks?

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) at a meeting of the IMF and the World Bank spoke out very strongly against

Canada's aid policy. The minister suggested that not only should aid not be increased, but that it should be diminished. Somehow or other the message got to the Secretary of State for External Affairs because her speech at the Empire Club might well have been written by another hand-

speechtext: By the slasher.

speechtext:
-compared to her speech at the United Nations. In any event, the message got to her or, to mix the metaphor, a terrified mouse came into her office pursued by the financial cat from Newfoundland to tell her that it was no longer possible for Canada to continue its aid policy of the past, and that it must now only look to countries on the brink of self-sufficiency.
In this proposed switch the Secretary of State for External Affairs has bypassed CIDA's own twin objectives, the assistance of countries in the achieving of self-sufficiency and the meeting of basic human needs; in other words, concentration on the poorest in the poorest countries. These CIDA priorities were approved by the Science Council, the International Food Policy Institute and donor countries such as Sweden, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.
She also ignored the recommendations of the Pearson Commission, OECD, the North-South Institute, and her most knowledgeable colleague on these matters, the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), who is now also her parliamentary secretary. She ignored, as a friend of mine said, the many Canadians who are not ashamed to proclaim their humanitarian priorities, and whose support is so necessary if Canada is to live up to her proclaimed objectives.
She tried to excuse this change of approach toward the Third and Fourth World countries by accusing many Third World countries of having branded us as imperialists and, therefore, not worthy of Canadian interest and concern. Even if this were true, that they had branded us as imperialists, 1 hardly think that this should be the reason for deciding to no longer care about the poorest in the poorest countries. But I am told that her comment that Pakistan led the attack of the non-aligned countries in Havana is not in fact true, that Pakistan did not lead the attack on the so-called imperialist countries. Even if the remarks were true, it is a pretty feeble reason to give for changing one's full approach to foreign aid.
The minister also indicated, as had the Minister of National Defence (Mr. MacKinnon) some time earlier, that we should take another look in our role in peacekeeping, presumably also to save money, presumably also because we are a nation that cannot afford enterprises such as peacekeeping any more than the level of aid that we have been giving. To suggest that we take another look at peacekeeping, particularly in Cyprus where there are 30,000 Turkish troops at present, is to me highly irresponsible.
It is because of these conflicts among members of the government on matters of foreign aid and peacekeeping, as well as on the embassy question, that the government presum-
The Address-Miss Jewett
ably decided to say nothing about international affairs in the Speech from the Throne and the Prime Minister decided to say nothing about it in his own speech. We are told that a standing committee of the House of Commons will have a report from the Department of External Affairs referred to it.
1 certainly do not deplore that; on the contrary, there will be useful discussions. That does not save the minister from saying now, in October, what direction we should be moving in- preferably not conflicting directions. We want a foreign policy not only for the 1980s but right now. We want some indication of where the government is going.

This is a country which has had a democratic revolution, the very kind of country that Canada should befriend after it has gone through this democratic process. At that time we had provided only three Hercules aircraft, I think-

-three Hercules flights to carry the economic aid and other supplies provided by the private sector in Canada, chiefly by the Canadian labour movement. I received a letter from the minister yesterday saying that this aid has now been increased to five flights carrying $400,000 worth of material, again mainly provided by the Canadian labour movement. She said:
I had hoped to be able to provide you with details of planned reconstruction efforts in addition to our emergency relief activities but I am not in a position to do so yet. speechtext:
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say on a happier note how very kind and generous with their time were the embassies in Tokyo and Peking when I recently took a trip there under the leadership of Tommy Douglas. We thought very highly of the staff of the embassies in those two capitals. On our trip we discovered that there is a marvellous opening for Canada in trade with these two countries.
It is my own feeling that the government has not been pushing our trade with Japan very strongly and has not made any inroads at all in what will become a huge market in China except, of course, with wheat and rape seed. Trade is a two-way street and there are many kinds of goods that the Chinese could provide to us, but at the moment, as hon. members know, we export far more to China than they export to us. Not only should we encourage trade with China, a

October 12, 1979
The Address-Miss Jewett
country that should appeal to the minister because, although it has a very low standard of living, it is on the brink of self-sufficiency, but we should extend our relations in one particular and important area, that of our scientific and technical knowledge.
The Chinese spoke to us about this a great deal and gave the example of gold mining, which is only half as efficient in China as it is in Canada, as well as oil extraction and reforestation. They would also like to develop even further the program now under way of exchanging students, scholars and experts between our universities. I would ask the minister to facilitate this program by ensuring that exchange scholars from China can have their health certificates approved quickly. I talked to one Chinese scholar on September 21 who was two weeks overdue at his post in Canada because he had been waiting three months for final approval of his health certificate from our mission in Hong Kong. Why does everything have to go to Hong Kong, already a very busy mission? Surely it would not be too difficult to attach a medical doctor to our embassy in Peking. If we are serious about this interchange of students and scholars, that is what should be done.
I hope that when the standing committee is established a coherent set of policies will be placed before it, policies in which all members of the government concur. I hope to play as constructive a role as I can on that committee and, through its efforts, to see Canada take an even greater lead in its relations, in its aid, in its trade with other countries that are on the brink of self-sufficiency as well as those that are still poor.
There is one other matter of importance to me and, I hope, to all members of the House, Mr. Speaker, that I should like to address this afternoon. At least there was one sentence about it in the Speech from the Throne, which is better than nothing at all. It was promised that there will be an employment strategy for women. I was very glad to hear that and will be glad to see it fleshed out.
It concerns me, however, that during the four and one-half months the government has been in office it has not done any of the things it promised in the election campaign. When the government referred to women in the public service during their election campaign they promised that the reduction in the federal public service would have no disproportionate effect on women, as had been the case under the Liberal government. In February, 1979, the number of women laid off was greater than the percentage they formed of the work force in every single branch of the public service. The same seems to be happening now although it is too early yet for all the details to be known. I mentioned one case yesterday where 12 women in the agricultural stabilization board have been laid off. One can find examples everywhere. What did the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) mean when he said yesterday:
Our guideline is no lessening of the number of women working in the public service.
That is simply not what is happening. Obviously he does not know what is happening to women in the public service. Perhaps he does not care.
A second example is women and the unemployment insurance amendments. Referring again to the campaign literature of the Progressive Conservative Party, and 1 am speaking of its document about strategy for women, it refers to the previous government, and I quote:
The government's changes to unemployment insurance eligibility discriminated significantly against women at the same time as the level of benefits received by persons such as single parents was reduced.
According to this article the Progressive Conservative Party will
(a)	keep the existing eligibility criteria for part-time and seasonal workers, who are disproportionately women, and
(b)	maintain the existing level of benefits for men or women with dependents.
That promise was violated immediately after the election.
I am particularly concerned in what this government is doing, following in the footsteps of the previous government, in eventually eradicating the Outreach program as it affects women. The outreach program has been one of the most successful programs we have had. It is a program designed to meet the special needs of women entering or re-entering the labour force. It has trained, counselled and placed a large number of women who had been on social assistance most of their lives. There is one Outreach program in my own constituency, called AWARE, which has trained, counselled and placed hundreds and hundreds of women. Indeed, in British Columbia and the Yukon together the number of women reached by the Outreach program is 6,000. They have been trained and placed at a cost of $250 per job placement while the Canada Employment Centre cost is $700 to $800 a person. The Conservative party have said:
A Progressive Conservative government will restore the necessary funding ($3 million) cut by the Trudeau government from the Department of Employment's Outreach program for women.
The government has restored $300,000. It has said that there will be an additional amount up to $1.3 million, but the government will not say whether this is for the Outreach program for women, the special program for women and their special needs. The government has said nothing that I am aware of about the remaining $1.7 million.
So many of these programs have been cut back that there are only about half a dozen left. One is in my constituency and I believe there is one in the constituency of my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller). No one knows whether these programs will be retained or not. What is so incredibly shortsighted about this is not only the unfairness to women, but the fact that the government will pay more for social assistance and unemployment insurance-if it does not cut back unemployment insurance even more-than it would pay to train and help these women enter the labour force. Even on the sort of "hacker grounds" you would not abandon this program.
The government also promised, again in its pre-campaign literature, that it would strengthen the role of the National


October 12, 1979
Advisory Council on the Status of Women. On page 5 of that literature the following is to be found:
The advice of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women is frequently ignored by government, most recently on the changes to unemployment insurance policy. We will first improve the credibility of the council by seeking nominations to its board from national women's organization.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker; I shall not crave your indulgence too much longer.
There have been no new appointments yet to fill the vacancies on the National Advisory Council. I respect very highly the Secretary of State (Mr. MacDonald), another good friend, and I know he is personally sympathetic to strengthening the role of the council. I am sure he is sympathetic to developing the Outreach program and genuinely changing the unemployment insurance amendments. Is he having any influence, inner cabinet or no inner cabinet, when he has not yet been able to change those matters or to put people on the council? Nor has there been any additional money granted to the council, as I understand was promised them some time ago.
The government also said in its election campaign literature that it would further provide that the council report directly to Parliament on any legislation or lack thereof which it feels is of importance to the status of Canadian women. Nothing has yet been said about that.
There are a number of matters I could raise. One need only read the recent report on women and poverty to learn that 16 per cent of adult women in Canada live in poverty. This government said it would address that problem so as to bring about genuine equality of women. Next week is persons' week. This is the week commemorating the famous persons decision when the judicial committee of the privy council said that "women" were "persons", yet the backward steps that seem to have been taken by the government set us back further even than in the last few years under the Liberal administration, which really gave up doing anything after international women's year. As members of parliament we must address ourselves at last to treating women as persons, not as secondary wage earners, not as uninterested people that you can push around, as was done recently in Ontario. Of course, the Tories are in power in that province and that government has just voted that domestics should not come under the minimum wage regulations.
I hope that the minister and the other ministers concerned, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) and the President of the Treasury Board, will at last give substance to their campaign rhetoric.
The Address-Mr. Chretien
