speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate you most sincerely on your re-election as Speaker of this House. It is a most happy precedent for the House to have decided to re-elect a member who served it so well in the previous Parliament. I would also like to offer my most sincere congratulations to the officers of this House and to yourself, Mr. Speaker, and my best wishes in your new responsibilities. I also wish to congratulate the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Nearly 16 years ago, when I was a new member, I myself had the opportunity to play the same role and I was very proud for the voters of my constituency to have been chosen to make a speech and to be able to represent them in the House in the first moments of a new Parliament. I also wish to congratulate all the new ministers who have been appointed by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). During the last 12 years I was able to sit on the treasury benches, and I believe that we should give members opposite an opportunity to prove themselves. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) said, their task is certainly not an easy one and our role in this House is not necessarily to make their life any easier. For my part, I intend to co-operate with my hon. friends on the treasury benches, but it is to be expected that I might be somewhat mischievous at times because we have often seen in this House the people who are now on the treasury benches and who used to be on this side of the House take a malicious pleasure in keeping me in the House for hours and days at a time on points of order, questions of privilege or debates which took longer than I could give them in view of the work I had to do. I have no intention of being as extreme as they were and I will let them do their work as, having sat on the treasury benches for 12 years, I am well aware that ministers have a very difficult task and that we should give them as much sympathy and assistance as possible.

It is a tremendous pleasure and privilege for me to take part today in the throne speech debate. I must admit that for me and for many of my colleagues it is a strange experience to be sitting on this side of the House. I intend to enjoy completely this experience while I can, because the government's record to date suggests that we will be put back on the other side very quickly.
The Prime Minister told us that Canadians voted for his party because they wanted a change. That is exactly what they got. No political party ever changed so fast as the Tory party did between May 22 and May 23.
Do hon. members opposite remember something called the stimulative deficit? The people of Canada remember hearing about the stimulative deficit in the months preceding the election. The present Prime Minister told the electorate of Canada that the only way to revive the economy was to have

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. Chretien
more government spending and bigger tax cuts. He said that was the only way to produce the larger revenues which would eventually reduce our deficit. In other words, we could not hope to balance the budget somewhere down the road if we did not drive up the deficit now. I objected to that. 1 am very pleased that today they have come to realize that either they did not know what they were talking about or they were trying to mislead the population. Within two months of their election victory, the stimulative deficit was no more. It was an idea whose time had come and gone. Suddenly we need cutbacks.
I am sorry the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) is not here because, being from the province of Newfoundland, he was always on his feet complaining about the bad effect of cutbacks on that province. However, we suddenly need cutbacks in unemployment insurance and federal transfers to the provinces. We need to eliminate the universality of old age pensions. I could go on and on with the programs being slashed by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens).
In spite of all the great speeches made by the President of the Treasury Board over the past four months about all the programs he was going to slash and how he would bring everything under control, the headline in this morning's paper read "Ottawa deficit will jump by $500 million". For months we have been told that expenditures were being brought under control. The President of the Treasury Board blames this on the increase in the price of oil. We knew that last winter when the OPEC nations raised their prices.
In July the President of the Treasury Board made a pronouncement on the deficit. In August he did the same. Today we realize he did not know what he was talking about. Either he did not know how to forecast expenditures, or he has already lost control over the bureaucracy. Today he is telling us the deficit will be $500 million more than he said before.
Despite the fact we were facing an election, I stood in my place as minister of finance and stated that I was not going to try to buy the votes of Canadians, that even though we might be going to the polls we were prepared to face reality. The then leader of the opposition and all his friends talked about stimulative deficits, not cutting unemployment insurance and so on. Now that they are in power, they have completely changed their policies.
I cannot criticize the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) that much. He has now seen the truth. After waiting for months, I was pleased to see him rise in his place yesterday and say that he supported the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Under the act, the minister has to assume full responsibility for the actions of the governor of the bank. Despite the pressure I was under, I never tried to create the impression that I was not responsible. I always said that I subscribed to the policies of the governor because monetary policy comes under the government.
I wish the Minister of Finance well. I know he is finding it quite difficult. However, I was a bit embarrassed when he said that Mr. Bouey had his absolute confidence, that he had perfect confidence in the governor, because I am sure that Mr. 
Bouey is not yet out of the woods. The last person in whom the minister had perfect confidence was the former deputy minister of finance. As the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley) informed this House only yesterday, it was only a couple of hours after the minister expressed complete confidence in his deputy that the Prime Minister fired Mr. Hood.
As the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas stated, the minister was reduced to apologizing to his senior staff for having to place on them the burden of a new deputy minister, a man the minister did not choose, a man the minister did not want as a deputy minister. I like the new Minister of Finance very much, but to see him being humiliated like that in the first days of his tenure in office was unbelievable. I do not know of any minister of finance since I have been around, or even before, not Mr. Fleming, for example, who would have accepted being humiliated in that way by his prime minister.
You know, they used to talk about our Prime Minister's Office-there were supposed to be a lot of people in there who were running things and the ministries were not running things. In fact the new administration have increased the number in that office by 25, or something like that, and ministers nowadays do not even have the freedom in some cases, I am told, to choose their own executive assistants. It is unbelievable that a minister with responsibilities to discharge should be told by some guy from the Prime Minister's office whether a certain person is or is not acceptable to be in his office.
I was glad to see that the Minister of Finance took responsibility for the increase in the interest rate and gave his full support to the governor of the bank. That is the right decision. It reflected the position he had to take. He is responsible. If he does not agree with the governor he can write him a letter and give him instructions. There were a lot of people in Canada who, during the election campaign, gave credence to a speech made at his first press conference by the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister. During that conference he said that in the future a government under his leadership would rely not on monetary policy but on fiscal and budgetary policy-monetary policy would not be used to cure inflation. But the government has no chance. Today, after five months in office, the President of the Treasury Board has to admit that the deficit will be $500 million more than predicted. That leaves the government no room; the business community and the market will see that, despite all the great speeches he made about cutting expenditures, he has failed miserably.
I congratulate the government for permitting the opposition to raise this question in committee, because I should like to ask a few questions on the subject. But I hope the Minister of Finance will be given the free hand he needs in order to discharge his responsibility. This business of imposing upon him a deputy minister he did not want, creates a very bad precedent in the history of the ministry. It is one of the frustrations besetting a minister of finance to find that he has very little control over many of the problems with which he
October 12, 1979

must deal. Nevertheless, it is his responsibility to create the proper climate of confidence, a sense that matters are under control, and nothing could be more dangerous in any administration than to see the prime minister pull the rug out from under his minister of finance.
Of course there is no way in which a minister of finance can deal with inflation overnight, notwithstanding those who, during the last campaign, said there was. I went through that for two years. I do believe that, in order to give confidence to the nation, the Minister of Finance has to be in control of his ministry, and not be forced to have a deputy minister who was not his choice, not be forced to go to the senior people in his department and tell them "Sorry, but I don't control the department," to the point that even in his own office, I am told, an executive assistant or an assistant had been imposed on him. This is the way to destroy a minister of finance, and I urge the government to act more sensibly in this regard.
The minister has not produced a budget, and that is a big mistake. When I brought down my budget last November I did so in very difficult circumstances. We were going into an election within months-there was no choice-and 1 put forward a budget which was seen by many people as being very dangerous politically for a government in power. The leader of the opposition at that time was talking about a stimulative deficit and what not, but 1 stood firm. Since then, good results have flowed from that budget. We have seen the unemployment figures falling from month to month to a point which is the lowest in many years. We are reaping the benefit of the two budgets which were brought down, one in April, 1978, and the other in November, 1978. But I must tell the Minister of Finance that there is a big time lag between new initiatives and the point at which they are felt in the economy.
It was a great mistake for the government not to bring down a budget earlier adjusting to the new circumstances because, since my last budget, inflation in the world economy has risen sharply and there has been a huge increase in the price of oil bought from the OPEC nations. This increase has been much larger than was anticipated by most observers.
I remember being at a meeting of the World Bank in Washington almost exactly a year ago, and talking to my colleagues there. The feeling was that the price of oil would probably increase by some 10 per cent or 15 per cent, perhaps by 20 per cent. It was much more than that, and there were wide fluctuations in the open market which pushed the price very high, in some cases 40 per cent higher. This meant a big change in the economic postures of all the nations concerned, and the effect has driven the United States economy into what some people regard as deep recession. In this situation the government hesitates and cannot make up its mind on anything.
I feel sorry for the poor Minister of Finance who has to prepare a budget this month while the Prime Minister and the minister of energy are unable to agree on the price of oil as they attempt to please either Mr. Davis or Mr. Lougheed. And the poor Minister of Finance has to write a budget not knowing what the compensation to offset the price of that
The Address-Mr. Chretien
commodity in eastern markets will be. We do not yet know what the policy will be. I recall I was involved in changing the pricing policy a year ago for the month of January, when I felt it was my duty to ask the government of Alberta and other producers of oil not to increase the price of oil by $1 because we were under too much pressure from inflation. I talked with them, and eventually they agreed. Of course, there were some rumblings. Of course, there were unfavourable editorials in some parts of Canada. A lot of people gave me hell, but I didn't give a damn because I felt that the job required someone who was a bit thick-skinned and could "take it". But I would point out that we are now in October.
I heard the Prime Minister on television the other day. He did not know what was going to happen. I guess he had a plan-he was to come out last Sunday with news of a big agreement after he and Mr. Lougheed had met in Montreal. The meeting failed. There can be no doubt that, when you are the Prime Minister of Canada, when you are the leader of a national government, you have to arbitrate the differences which arise in this land. There is no way in which consensus will be reached, because it is not in the nature of things that Mr. Lougheed should say he doesn't want a higher price for Albertan oil-after all, he has to get elected in Alberta-and it is not in the nature of things for Mr. Davis to say he does not want a lower price. Eventually, the leader of a national government has to take a stand in the best interests of the nation as a whole. Of course ministers opposite have not done this, so the poor Minister of Finance will have been operating under my 13-month old budget before he brings in another.
Do not forget, Mr. Speaker, that these are the same people who were asking me last March when a budget would be brought down. As 1 say, we are already in October. They hope to give us a budget in a month or two, but the poor Minister of Finance has no clue about the probable cost to the treasury of maintaining the government's compensation program for oil imports. I hope he and his colleagues realize it is not possible to study these problems ad nauseam.
Mrs. Thatcher did not like the policies of the previous government in England. She moved, in the first week after her election, with a speech fron the throne. There was a budget within a month. I do not know whether it was a good one or a bad one, but she had some convictions and she showed them. Here we have the contrary.
For me it is rather a pleasure to be standing up here after so many months. Hon. members opposite have not found a way to change the policies we enunciated. They have fed for the last five months on my budget, which was supposed to be terrible. This is fun for me, but it is not fun for the nation. I know that there is a time lag of six months to a year before the effects of fiscal or budgetary measures are felt in the economy. Results do not happen overnight. On the night of a budget big pronouncements can be made, but it takes six months or a year before millions and millions are affected by the implementation of measures.

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. Chretien
By the time we have a new budget it will already be too late, because we have known since the month of April that the Americans are in a recession.There was a big debate among all the economists of the world as to whether the Americans were or were not going into a recession. Now it is evident that they were. Perhaps the Tories will be happy to see the Canadian economy go into a recession, but I would like to tell them that it is not necessary. Even if there is a recession in the United States now, for 27 months during the last recession in the United States we managed to maintain some growth in the Canadian economy. It was not enough, but there was some growth.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister promised that there would be an average rate of growth of 5.5 per cent should he come into power. Yet right away we are told that it looks as though, next year, growth will be under 2 per cent. Hon. members opposite were going to reduce the deficit, but it will be $500 million higher. It would be better for hon. members opposite to tell the truth to the people.
During the campaign we said that there was no room to make promises. That was not easy. I wish we could have made promises. Perhaps we lost the election, but I am proud that, despite the fact we did not make many promises during the campaign, we got more votes than the present government, and we kept our respectability. I do not see much respectability in the present government.

And now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to devote a few minutes to federal-provincial relations, a new field assigned to me by the Leader of the Opposition. I was pleased to accept, because I believe that we are now going through a very dangerous period in Canada. However, I am somewhat discouraged when I see the government believing that with appeasing policies, they will succeed in solving problems in the area of federal-provincial relations, especially when we Canadians in Quebec where most of us are Canadians know that in a few months we will have to vote in the referendum. In addition, we are being told by the Prime Minister of Canada that since he may have concluded an agreement on Loto Canada-it has not yet been ratified-that problem of relations between Quebec and the remainder of Canada will be solved. It is a big joke, Mr. Speaker. What was the matter with Loto Canada? It is an organization which the federal government had set up specifically to help the province of Quebec because of the Olympic Games deficit and which, therefore, is not a provincial responsibility. In order to make the first lottery possible in Canada, the Parliament of Canada had to introduce legislation and amend the Criminal Code to allow Jean Drapeau to hold his Olympic lottery, and as this scheme was to expire in the month of August following the Olympic Games, I personally introduced in the House a bill calling for the continuation of the scheme. And now the government is talking about turning it over to the provinces and trying to negotiate a return of the money from the provinces to the federal government.

Mr. Speaker, I hear that one of the stumbling blocks which is delaying the signing of the agreement-I can hardly believe it-is the fact that the province of Quebec, although willing to take part in a lottery with the other provinces, does not want it to be called Loto Canada, because the word Canada is there. And the Progressive Conservative government agrees on that. It is Loto Canada. I am not ashamed to say it. I am a Canadian. I like the word "Canada", and most people in Quebec like it; it represents the obstacle to the settlement of, that little problem.
I could talk about the other so-called successes of the right hon. Prime Minister in the area of federal-provincial relations, namely, offshore rights. He made a nice gift to the provinces. He kept six or eight jurisdictions for the federal government. Furthermore, it will be necessary to amend the constitution. In another case either they give or they do not. And why have that debate which is going to create all kinds of controversies while governments concerned, besides the federal government, found a formula which avoided the conflict of jurisdictions, and which was found to be very favourable by the provinces? Even today, the Conservative premier of New Brunswick, Mr. Hatfield, says he is not convinced that the action taken by the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada is really in the interest of the maritimes, because even if they have oil revenues they are going to lose on equalization payments. So as the saying goes, they will have changed "four quarters for a dollar". They may not have gained anything. But in the meantime there are oil companies that want to search for oil at this point in that area, and they find themselves in the situation where one holds a provincial licence, while another holds a federal licence for the same area. There will be no oil finds there for quite some time because of that hassle. And if they are in doubt because of a constitutional amendment we will have to go to London and have the agreement of all provinces because the Prime Minister stated he would never amend the constitution without agreement from all provinces. So that situation will prevail for months. People in Newfoundland will believe they got a gift, but the Prime Minister will be unable to deliver.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will have an opportunity to come back on this. First I would extend my best wishes to the Minister of Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Jarvis). This is a very difficult task, and I know he is committed to devoting all his energy and talent. So I wish him good luck. However, as I said on the oil situation, that kind of problem will never be solved through some kind of meeting where everyone is in agreement. This is impossible by the very nature of things. If you are the mayor of a community and have a problem, you blame the provincial government. If you are a provincial premier and have a problem, you blame the federal government. But we up here, Mr. Speaker, we cannot blame the Queen of England. Occasionally we blame the Americans, when we have a chance. All that is in the nature of things. So I wish him good luck, but at some point he will have to face the
October 12, 1979

facts and say, "We are the government, and must take a decision in the interest of all Canadians".
I should like to deal for a few minutes with one of the attitudes of the party in power which concerns me greatly. We held a debate in this House before the election on the bill we had introduced dealing with referendums: the bill gave the federal government the power to hold referendums. Both the Progressive Conservatives and the New Democrats supported the measure, the Conservatives saying, "We do not want the bill in that form but will accept a referendum on the Quebec issue". Today, the Prime Minister claims that by withdrawing his own plan for a referendum, he has done what was needed to incite Quebeckers to remain Canadians. Come on! That is sheer naivete. What is the number one priority of the Parti Quebecois program? What is it? To separate Quebec from Canada. They are trying to find some formula or other, just the way they did in the last election, to trick the voters. They got themselves elected then by saying, "Now, we will give you good government/' Then, they spent the last three and a half years talking only about separation and getting ready for it. Now they are free. We set them free and enabled them to put the question they want to ask. They want a mandate to negotiate something or other. Only after the election will Mr. Levesque tell us exactly what that mandate is. What worries me is that 1 have heard several hon. members opposite say that they have a plan. That plan, believe it or not, is that if the question is not the right one, they will come in at the last minute with a bill. That will be provocation of the worst kind! For months they will have worn the mask of the jolly good fellow, of the pleasant guy. Then, when there is maximum tension in Quebec, without notice, without warning, they will club them with a federal referendum. Why not be honest with the people of Quebec? If Mr. Levesque asks an honest question, there will be no problem.

speechtext: He will be beaten.

speechtext:
He will be beaten. But the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. LaSalle) knows full well that he will not ask an honest question. He knows that and I am happy to hear him say so.
But get ready, because there are millions of citizens in Quebec who want to stay in Canada. There are some 680,000 to 700,000 Anglophones there. I met a few in Montreal recently who were telling me that they felt totally abandoned, that they at least had the hope that the Government of Canada would assume its responsibility to protect them in this debate, where they feel like floating in a nutshell over a stormy sea, but that now, in an attempt to smooth things over, they were being totally neglected. There is nothing wrong with having a bill here, at the federal level, which, if Mr. Levesque's question is honest, can be left dormant, but to come at the last minute, underhandedly, that is dishonest towards the people of Quebec.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to address this august House. First I should like to congratulate Your Honour on your appointment to position of Speaker. It is a high office, and it goes without saying that I will abide by Mr. Speaker's rulings. I am sorry the last speaker, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), has left so soon because I have a message for him.

speechtext:
I should like to speak for a moment about the Speech from the Throne. We have heard comments indicating that it was not much of a speech, that there was nothing in it. I was delighted with it. It was a positive speech. It emphasized what we on this side said during the election campaign. Throughout my remarks I will bring that out.
Canadians today are looking for credibility. In short that is what defeated the last government, the lack of credibility. Canadians are looking to a government which will set policies that will be carried on for some time in the future, so that industrialists and entrepreneurs can make their plans and go ahead with them. That will be a change from what they have had in the past.
The riding of Kamloops-Shuswap was named for its two beautiful lakes. I should like to thank personally the voters of that constituency for choosing me to be their representative here and for the confidence they have placed in me, confidence which I do not take lightly. Kamloops is the regional centre of the south central part of British Columbia. The Trans-Canada highway and the Yellowknife highway pass through it. Also it is a divisional point on both the CN and CP railways. It has a large shopping centre or district upon which 130,000 people depend. Approximately 60,000 people live in the town of Kamloops itself. Salmon Arm is a small town on the banks of Shuswap Lake. It is a beautiful spot, it is a beautiful lake. The active industries in that part of the country are forestry, mining, agriculture, ranching, tourism, and some light industry. I should like to spend most of my time talking about these industries.

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. Cameron
There are three producing mines in this area. In the case of two mines they export their concentrate, and in the case of the third one it is smelted down and they export approximately an 1,100-pound ingot. The primary metal is copper. There is molly, as it is known in the industry, or molybdenum, with something more than trace elements of gold and silver in the area. Since May 22, which is an interesting date to note, one new mine has started. At present they are stripping overburden, pouring concrete, erecting steel, and putting up a new concentrater. The new mine is bigger than any two of the three operating at the moment. Also heavy equipment is moving into the area to begin construction of another new mine which will be larger than all the others put together. This shows the confidence industrialists have in the present government. They have known of this ore for several years. It has sat in the ground, it has never been developed. Studies have been done on it and there have been drilling reports which have sat there for years. Since May 22 the industrialists have confidence in the government because they know its policies, and they are going ahead.
I should like to refer to a newspaper clipping which I received today from the area. It reads as follows:
Anderson, formerly Afton Mines mine manager, estimates that full development by all four copper mining companies would mean a combined annual payroll of $56 million for 2,600 persons employed in the mining industry in the Highland Valley by 1982.
Also I should like to refer to some specifics respecting what these mines produce. The milling capacity of Afton Mines Limited is 8,500 tons of ore per day. Its annual production is just over 57 million pounds of copper. Also it produces just under 58,000 ounces of gold and 290,087 ounces of silver. In the case of Bethlehem Copper, its milling capacity is 20,000 tons per day. Its annual production is 47,761,191 pounds of copper and just under 500,000 pounds of molybdenum.
In the case of Lornex, its mining capacity is 48,100 tons per day. Its annual production is 135,422,000 pounds of copper and 3,985,000 pounds of molybdenum. Perhaps these figures do not seem like very much, but in the industry what that adds up to is quite substantial and relieves some of our balance of payments.
British Columbia produces over $450 million worth of the copper which is sold on the export market per year. It produces over $45 million worth of gold a year. It produces just under 30 million pounds of molybdenum which is worth over $160 million a year. This has a very good effect on our balance of payments.
In this country we have so much in the way of resources, in greater quantities than in almost any other country in the world. We have the skills and the know-how to develop and to extract those resources, whether they be timber or minerals. One of our problems is that most people, and I say "most", cannot see the trees for the forest. It is to be hoped, now that we have a change in government and that more positive, long-range plans are in effect for the industrialists, that we will have greater participation by them in these industries.

The forestry industry in our area is a primary economic producer. We have ten large sawmills and one pulp mill employing a force of about 9,300 people. This industry produces an export commodity that we ship in great quantities, helping to relieve our balance of payments.
We also have tourism in the area. It is a great hunting, fishing, skiing, and sports area. I am sorry that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) is not here as he would be interested in this. A couple of years ago he was out in our area and skied at a place called Todd Mountain. Two entrepreneurs have taken over this area and spent $1.5 million improving it this year. They started out in a business-like manner. They had Snow Engineering carry out their study, the same people who designed the Aspen, Colorado development. They found that we have greater potential on Todd Mountain than in Aspen, Colorado.
These people have located and marked 21 ski runs on the mountain. I am pleased to say that the mountain will not be denuded of its trees. The course will be cut down the mountain with trees left between the different runs. There will be slopes for beginners, for the average person, and for the expert. They are also planning to build a lodge at the foot of the ski lifts to accommodate people while in the area. They have installed a third lift in there this year. I had the privilege of driving over the new ski run with them. They have cleared an area some 200 feet in width which is tapered on both sides and curves down the mountain. This is an excellent area. It has been raked free of boulders by hand, and sown in grass, so that with three, four or six inches of snow people will be able to use the runs.
That is the kind of thing I want to see developed. I am not interested in handout projects for the riding. Much more is to be gained through private enterprise, with government-set stable conditions so that entrepreneurs can go ahead and make their plans. Let us put private industry to work, as I am sure this will pay great returns.
I am sorry the hon. member for Saint-Maurice is not here as he had some direction in respect of what I wish to talk about now. There is a railway relocation problem in the riding of Kamloops-Shuswap. This is a problem that goes back a number of years to when the then minister of transport, Mr. Lang, decided there should be a rail relocation study. Certainly in respect of railway relocations Kamploops and Regina are the two worst cities in the country.
The former government said we should go ahead and conduct a study. The former minister said to spend up to $200,000 with the government paying half and the area paying half. That was fine, and we went ahead with the study. As it was nearing completion we experienced one of the customary restraint programs, and there was no more money. Within a month or so the former government made another promise, saying there would be money and we should complete the study. The former minister said that we were so near to completion and that this was such valuable information we should go ahead and the money would be forthcoming. We went ahead, completed the study and turned the study over to
October 12, 1979

the government. Again we experienced a restraint program, and again no money was forthcoming. To this date that small city of Kamloops is stuck with that cost of $100,000, the federal government's share of the bill which the former government left hanging. Surely that is a poor way to establish any kind of co-operation or to get negotiations going. This is a very sad situation.
Let me make a few remarks about a prison that was to be established in the area. This was first suggested some four or five years ago. A former solicitor general came out and announced that the government was going to build a prison in the Kamloops area. There is nothing else in the world that we need like we need a prison. We were told to pick out a site, and a site was chosen. The government purchased 38 acres up on the west hill just at the edge of Kamloops. They could have chosen a site a lot further out and still been within the city boundaries. In any event, the government bought this 38-acre site for $160,000. It did not seem to make any difference that there was a crude oil pipeline running through the area. Nor did it matter that there was a natural gas pipeline running through the same area along with a hydro line. We were told this was no problem and the government would have them moved. The federal government moved them and paid another $200,000.
I would like to know who owned that land. I did not bother to find out, but I could pretty well tell you who it was. We were told many times during the election campaign that the prison was to be built there. 1 am not all that enamoured with a prison in the area; 1 could live with it, or do without it, but certainly it should not be that close to the town. 1 am sure the people who made the decision in years gone by to establish the prison a number of miles outside New Westminster have now had after-thoughts. It is now located within city boundaries, and the people do not like it. There are many better places where a prison could be located than at that spot in Kamloops.
Another matter I should like to refer to, Mr. Speaker, relates to the airport at Kamloops. We have our problems at the airport. Kamloops is situated in the bottom of the river valley in that area. We have a pulp mill on one side of the airport and a refinery on the other. We do experience some air inversion in winter, and quite often we have over-flights. I think there were 29 in the month of December last year.
This matter was judiciously brought up during the last election campaign. We were told we were going to get some improvements to our airport almost immediately. We were given to understand the improvements would be started even before the vote. The amount involved started at $1.1 million, increased to $2 million, then to $2.5 million, and finally $2.95 was settled on. We heard other figures up to $5.5 million and $6 million. Needless to say, nothing has been done. The money was set aside in the budget but, as a previous member, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), has said, what the government failed to do was go to Treasury Board and obtain approval.
Those are some of the facts I picked up when I took over in the area. Another situation that was brought to my attention
The Address-Mr. Cameron
relates to the Thompson River system. This system includes the two lakes for which the riding is named. It also includes the two Thompson rivers. The North Thompson flows generally from the area of Jasper, and joins the South Thompson at Kamloops. The South Thompson flows from Shuswap Lake. The river then flows down to Lytton where it joins the Fraser.
Studies have been done on the Thompson River system for as long as we have had studies, and 1 think we could produce almost any type of study you would care to see. The thing that the people of my riding are concerned about is the condition of the water in the Thompson and Fraser rivers all the way down to the coast.
In B.C. most cities are unable to get water by drilling. They pump their water out of the rivers. At one time it was good drinking water, but today most of the towns along the Shuswap, Kamloops, and most of the towns down along the Thompson and Fraser system, dump their sewage into it. It was announced during the election that we would have a $60,000 pre-planning study done on the problem. We are in the throes of receiving that report now, and if there is one point I would like to make today emphatically it is that we do not need any more studies on the Thompson River. In the first place, we did not need studies to tell us not to dump sewage into the rivers, we needed action.
That river system is also the run for the famous Pacific sockeye salmon. They come up the Fraser River into the Thompson River, into the Shuswap and into the Adams River and Adams Lake. It is one of the largest sockeye spawning runs in the world. In fact there is a sign along the run that advertises the one section of the run as the world's richest 300 acres. So, not only are the citizens of the area in danger, but the salmon are facing the danger of being wiped out.
I would like to speak for a moment about the Yellowhead highway system. I was pleased when the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) said that he was interested in having some of that highway system upgraded. The part I am interested in runs from Tete Jaune Cache down through Kamloops, on down to Merritt and over the whole Flope-Princeton highway. Generally speaking, it is a good highway, but there is a section from Kamloops north for some 40 miles to Barriere, and in particular a 15-mile section within the boundaries of Kamloops, which is now approaching an unstable condition at speed levels of 30 miles per hour. This is from the Pacific Rim highway study. The traffic on that road is not ordinary traffic. The grades on that highway for truckers going to and from the prairies are the best we have through British Columbia. There is only one bad hill to pull in the whole system. Consequently all the heavy freight trucks use it, to say nothing of the log trucks, approximately 100 of them a day, and 1 would venture as many chip trucks in a 24 hour period. These trucks carry in the vicinity of 80,000 to 90,000 pound loads or, in other words, 40 to 45 tons. To have loads like that travelling a highway which is approaching an unstable condition at speed levels of 30 miles an hour is hardly a situation we appreciate.

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. Cameron
I would like to say a few words now about energy, and in particular Petro-Canada. We have heard on several occasions from both parties opposite about Petro-Canada. It is only right that they should explain their side of the coin, but there are two sides to every coin. I would like to take a moment to run over our side now.
If my memory serves me correctly, and I believe that it does, Petro-Canada was originally set up when we had a minority government. In fact only yesterday they were talking about a paternity suit over it, and maybe there will be a divorce later and an alimony suit later. When PetroCan was set up with the use of taxpayer's money in the amount of approximately $1 billion, I can remember reading the reports each year in Hansard before I came to the House, and the government of the day would seem to come at budget time for $200 million to $250 million for running expenses. That was fine. Then they started acquiring some properties. The first thing that was done was that Petro-Canada began buying up shares in pipeline companies or oil companies, shares which you and I or some senior citizen might well have had and from which they could get a small dividend, while some portion of it flowed to the treasury. However, we do not have that today. The company bought up the shares and they are going into a conglomerate. The NDP are always talking about multinationals and conglomerates. This company is approaching that size.
The NDP also talk about having a window on the oil industry in order to know what is going on. From what I hear from the NDP and the Liberal party, when they get down to have a look in that window they must have their rose-coloured glasses on. I have not heard any reports about the oil Petro-Canada is producing. The purchase of Pacific Petroleums has not produced one drop of oil for Canada, and it is the same with the other oil company which was purchased. Petro-Canada has not produced any oil for Canada in order that it may have shares in the pipeline, shares away from which the government of the day pushed some poor little senior citizen. That has not helped Canada.
I am interested to hear from the NDP spokesman on what that party's policy is on uranium. During the election they said that there would be no mining of uranium in British Columbia.
I guess the party has taken a different position in Saskatchewan, but that is their problem. Their leader went across the country on what he called a crusade, but I noticed that he was always speaking to the committed, the unions and so on, saying that Petro-Canada must be kept. It is interesting to note that one of the subsidiaries of Petro-Canada is busy in B.C. exploring for uranium in the area of Peachland, Penticton, and up toward Merritt. Apparently they are also interested in buying claims in the Adams Plateau. I am sure that we over here would all like to know just what their position is on that matter.
There is another angle to Petro-Canada with which I am not happy. No Canadian would object to the taxpayers' money being spent to find oil in the north or on the heavy oil in the sands on the Saskatchewan-Alberta border, nor do they particularly object to the importing of oil from other countries.

But I am sure they do object to their money being spent through Petro-Canada on drilling for oil in Pakistan, off the Norwegian coast, or in China. It will not produce one drop of oil for Canada. Those are some of the things on the other side of the coin, and the things which the parties opposite missed when they were looking through the window on the energy industry.
I have emphasized some of the characteristics of the Kamloops area, the beautiful climate and the once beautiful farming country. I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) about the agricultural lands, particularly the better classes of soil which are fast disappearing. Kamloops is a prime example. We once had on the north shore of the Thompson a beautiful flat that was all in orchards producing beautiful crops. But today there is only one small orchard of some 15 or 20 acres left. The whole area is now housing. I certainly think that the hon. member's remarks were to the point and worth considering, and I agree with him.
Lastly, I would like to say that my riding of Kamloops-Shuswap is proud to be part of this great Canada, this Canada from sea to sea, and we certainly believe that it should and will stay as one country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was beginning to feel a little like a jumping jack, getting up and down. If the other business has been concluded I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and all the members here because it is a genuine honour to give my first address in this chamber. It is a chamber with a great deal of history. Anyone coming here feels that history and cannot help but be honoured by the process that brought him. In my case I want to thank the voters of Vancouver Centre for the landslide victory they gave me. I had 94 more votes than I really needed to be elected and I appreciate every one of them. I want to assure all the voters of Vancouver Centre, even the 65 per cent who voted against me, that I am going to do my best for them in this chamber.
I understand it is traditional to speak about one's riding at this time and tell everyone what a fine place it is. As a former mayor of Vancouver I certainly know the riding well. I love it and I enjoy speaking about it. I see the former mayor of Toronto sitting opposite as a minister of the government, and I am sure he shares these feelings.
I have found, however, that it is not a good idea to tell people of all the virtues of Vancouver. When we do that we find that easterners somehow descend on it. We refer to anybody beyond the Rocky Mountains as easterners, of course. Those from Alberta are mid-easterners, and I think the House is beginning to understand, as is the country, why we refer to them that way. People who live beyond Alberta are referred to as far easterners. When all these people find out the truth about our city, they flock to it. They crowd our beautiful, unpolluted sandy beaches, and Stanley Park which is partly in my riding. They jam the ski slopes just 15 minutes away from my riding which, unfortunately, are represented by two members on the other side, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). They will be ably represented, I am sure. In any case, Mr. Speaker, visitors come flocking. The virtues of Vancouver attract them too well, so the best thing is to say nothing. For that reason I will say no more about it tonight.
I should like to speak about a part of my riding that is of great national importance, and that is the port of Vancouver. I see the Postmaster General and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Fraser) who represents Vancouver South, and other members who represent parts of greater Vancouver, in the House, and I am sure they will agree, as would members from the prairies and other parts of Canada, that the port of
The Address-Mr. Phillips
Vancouver is a national institution of great importance to us all. During the time I was mayor of the city, and since, I have wanted to see changes in the administration of the port. Unfortunately, it has been a long distance administration over the years, coming under the authority of the National Harbours Board in Ottawa. That is simply not the best type of administration for a local port which should have more local input and more local autonomy. There is a very fine port manager, but the port needs to have more control over its own affairs in the area, and this is one of the interests I propose to pursue in this House.
I know bills have been brought before the House in earlier days which would give a great deal of local control to the port of Vancouver, but they have not been passed. I hope that members from the other parties will join with those who represent the greater Vancouver area in trying to bring about this important and necessary change at the port of Vancouver for the benefit of the city of Vancouver and for the benefit of all Canadians. We feel saddened when we see the port of Seattle taking away some of our container business because our port has lagged behind in development. We feel we can do better. In my judgment this is a non-partisan issue and one that I would like to pursue with the other parties in this House.
I believe there are many occasions in this House when members can pursue issues in a non-partisan fashion while representing regional interests. I should like to do more of that myself as it fits in with my municipal background.
I believe we should be providing this type of constructive opposition. Our leader has commented many times that our role is to provide such constructive opposition-criticizing when there are things to criticize, and certainly the government has given us many such occasions so far, and there will be others-but offering constructive suggestions and positive proposals from the position of opposition.
The Liberal opposition has been organized in the form of a number of caucus committees. It is my great pleasure to be chairman of the committee on resources and small businesses. The resources involved, mining and forestry, are of great importance to British Columbia and western Canada. The small business aspect fits in very well with my personal background in business, small business and finance. I am delighted to represent those areas in the opposition and look forward to participating in the debates.
The hon. member who spoke ahead of me referred to mining and forestry in Kamloops, the area he represents, and said that both industries are strong. It is true that both are doing well. In the case of mining, however, stable taxation policies are needed so that those involved in it know where they stand and do not have surprises sprung upon them.
The forestry industry is also in good shape. It is true that the lower Canadian dollar has helped it a good deal, as has the task force established by the previous government. There is a great need for further reforestation programs, Mr. Speaker, if this country is not to run out of timber by the end of this century, and plans should be laid for them. You cannot suddenly just plant 100-foot trees. This is an area in which I

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. Phillips
want to see the government take further action. There was considerable improvement as a result of the task force initiated by the previous federal government. Joint federal-provincial programs are catching up part of that backlog, but more needs to be done.
I want to talk about small business for a moment. Small business is growing and flourishing in Canada. What many of us forget is that two-thirds of the job growth in the last five years has come from small business. Small business has been doing well. There has been quite an upsurge in the feeling of entrepreneurship among young people in their late twenties and early thirties. What you are seeing is the "do your own thing" generation reaching an age where they want to do their own thing, but they also want to earn a good living doing it. There is no better way of doing your own thing and earning a good living while doing it, than being your own boss and in your own small business.
1 am delighted to see people taking a greater interest in running their own businesses. There is a shortage of entrepreneurship in this country, but this is improving. There is a great interest in the colleges and community colleges in courses designed to help people run their own businesses. We must encourage that and ensure that sort of thing is easier for people to do. There is no greater freedom, creativity, pure fun as well as opportunity than one can find in running one's own business. However, it is tough to get started.
About 60 per cent of small businesses fail in their first try. Small businessmen starting something usually fail, and that is a great pain. Instead of giving government handouts to people in order to encourage them to go into business, because that type of thing is almost impossible to administer at the very small business level, we can ease that pain to some extent. We can do this by looking at better capital loss right-offs for small businessmen initiating their own small businesses-starting their own businesses and failing. That is part of the process. A lot of us have scars to show that we have started some businesses and failed. If we can ease that pain, we could get many more people started in the system at relatively low cost to the treasury.
I have seen proposals for a $5,000 tax credit for investment in small businesses. I have seen proposals from the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Chamber of Commerce, and others. We on this side concur with that idea. The former prime minister suggested in the last election campaign a $5,000 tax credit for people investing in their own businesses, for example by buying shares in their own businesses for employees. This is easily extendible to people starting in a new business of their own, and is a worth-while idea for the government to pursue.
The Federal Business Development Bank has been an instrument of great benefit to small business people. It has not made money because its mandate is not to make money. It has broken even, which is what it should do. It has taken on high risk loans, made money available to small businessmen, and

enabled them to grow. It has been one of the primary sources of financing for small business.
I hear disturbing rumours that people want to cut back on this program. There is talk of privatizing part of it, of restricting it and making it into a much more profit-making organization. I suggest all this would destroy the mandate of the Federal Business Development Bank, and 1 do not want to see that happen. We on this side will fight any threat to restrict, cut back, shrink or privatize the Federal Business Development Bank. This is not because we are against privatization. We are not against privatization per se. We believe that the whole process of looking at government Crown corporations should be a selective one. We should look at corporations that have either been acquired or developed by the government and ask, are these still serving a function for the government, or are they not, and if they are not, would they be better sold to private enterprise in some way? We should look at this question selectively and not dogmatically. In that way I think we will find there are some cases.
The former government had intentions to return to private investors some of the companies that it owned. It bought Canadair, and a good thing it did too. Canadair was a very successful investment. It saved many jobs in Canada and it developed a viable industry. But there may come an occasion when it is sensible and when an appropriate buyer is available when that can be turned back to private industry. We have no objection to examining those sorts of things on their merits, and I think they should be examined.
There is one company we have examined on its merits and that is Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada should not be privatized. Privatizing that company is all wrong, and we oppose it in any form.
Petro-Canada has been a huge success. As the hon. member from the opposition who spoke before me mentioned, about $1 billion in taxpayers' money has been invested in Petro-Canada. True. That investment is now worth approximately $2 billion to $3 billion. Petro-Canada has been a fine investment and a fine use of taxpayers' money. In only four years it has grown to be the largest Canadian oil company operating in Canada. This company has taken high risks in the Arctic, offshore Labrador and so on. It has done very well. It has produced new fields of oil and it has helped solve some of our energy problems. It has been incredibly successful, no matter how you look at it. This company has even helped small business, Mr. Speaker.
Petro-Canada has come to the rescue of many independent retailers, particularly in the province of Quebec, who are being squeezed out of business by the large multinationals. It has come to the rescue and helped many independent oil producers in the province of Alberta who could not afford to participate in drilling syndicates under normal circumstances but who were pulled together by Petro-Canada, and assisted. It would be a tragedy to privatize Petro-Canada. It has been too good, and it is needed under government ownership.
The previous speaker mentioned that Petro-Canada had been started by the minority government. This is not so. The
October 12, 1979

bill was initiated, and royal assent was given under the majority government in late 1974, early 1975. The company was created by a majority Liberal government, expanded by a majority Liberal government to where it is now, and it has been one of the most successful undertakings of the previous Liberal majority government of the last five years.
I want to talk a little bit about the proposals to privatize Petro-Canada. There have been several proposals, and we are not sure where the government stands, whether it is to privatize part of it, all of it, to cut it up, keep the unprofitable parts for some obscure reason and sell off the good parts that turn a profit. All these sorts of plans have been heard and the question is now in the hands of a committee which, 1 understand, reports next week. One of the suggestions that I think will come out of this is to what we call "BCRIC" it.
Those of us who come from British Columbia know what "BCR1C" means. It refers to the British Columbia Resources Investment Company. This company was a corporation owned by the provincial government containing mainly forest products companies, some minority shareholdings, Westcoast Transmission, some oil and gas rights, and so on. It was a profitable, mature package, and it was turned over to individuals in the province of British Columbia by the provincial government in two ways. First, free shares were given to each resident of British Columbia, even to newly born babies; then each individual was given the right to buy up to approximately $30,000 of the stock additionally. This type of venture has been a tremendous success in British Columbia, and 1 personally applaud this whole approach. It was a success in two ways.
The investors poured in money far in excess of what people had expected. Almost $500 million came in when about $100 million was expected. Eighty-seven per cent of the citizens took advantage of their free shares. More than that, it has been a dramatic educational experience for residents of British Columbia. Every school child owns shares in BCRIC. They talk about it in the classrooms and thousands of citizens have, for the first time, become shareholders and investors in a viable corporation, namely, BCRIC. It has been an outstanding success.
This is a success that could be applied at the national level, but for PetroCan it is all wrong. For Petro-Canada this whole idea makes no sense, for a couple of reasons. Once a company is a shareholder company, it is a different kind of company. The interests of shareholders must be thought about and concern over potential dividends become important. A company is much more cautious once it becomes a shareholder company. It cannot afford to take the kinds of risks that this government-owned company has taken. It simply cannot do that. It requires government clout behind it to give it the kind of strength it needs to offset the fact that our oil industry is so totally dominated by foreign multinationals.
We do not need just another Canadian owned company. We need a company with clout. That is what we have. We now have a company that is an instrument of national policy. That
The Address-Mr. McMillan
is most important to remember at all times. This is an instrument of national policy. It has been highly successful.
Even Premier Bennett, who is not part of our party, said just the other day during a radio interview that to "BCRIC" PetroCan would make no sense. It makes no sense to "BCRIC" a company that is an instrument of national policy. Those were the words of Premier Bennett, and he knows of what he talks in this case. Elis advice should be heeded by members across the aisle when it comes to PetroCan.
I suggest there is a candidate for "BCRICing," the Canada Development Corporation. An article in the Journal a day or so ago suggested that this company is being considered for privatizing and turning back to private investors. I commend the government for considering that. It makes sense. This company is diversified in mining, petrochemicals, oil and gas. It has 32 per cent of its shares now held by individual investors. It is a shareholder company, not an instrument of government national policy.
The intention of the government at all times with the Canada Development Corporation has been to turn it back eventually to the private sector, reducing the government holding from 68 per cent to 10 per cent. They have embarked on that course. I suggest to the government that "BCRICing" PetroCan makes no sense, that it would just be a way to get out of an embarrassing commitment which all of us know is wrong. The public knows it is wrong, we know it is wrong, and you know in your hearts it is wrong. Do not "BCRIC" PetroCan. "BCRIC" the Canada Development Corporation. That makes sense.
If the government wants to add some other corporations that should be returned to the private sector, do so. That makes sense. You have a perfect vehicle; use it. The Liberals will support intelligent privatization. We will examine the Crown corporations to see which, if any, should be returned to the private sector. However, we will not support a dogmatic, narrow-minded approach which says that everything owned by the government should be privatized.
In the case of PetroCan every sensible observer, even Conservative observers such as the Globe and Mail, recognize that this company should be kept together, kept strong and an instrument of national policy. Don't "BCRIC," dismember, sell off or mess up PetroCan in any way. Show some vision. Have some pride in Canadian ownership of an outstanding Canadian enterprise. Keep PetroCan and expand it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by congratulating most heartily the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) on being chosen Speaker in this Parliament. His is a most difficult responsibility, which he performed admirably and with a great deal of distinction and grace in the previous House. I am sure all hon. members join me in wishing him well as he faces the substantial responsibilities that are produced because of our minority government situation.
1 congratulate as well the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon.
158

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. McMillan
member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald). Theirs were first-rate speeches which set a very high standard for every member of this House. If I may be allowed a personal note, Mr. Speaker, I was particularly delighted with the speech given by my friend and colleague from Prince Edward Island, the hon. member for Cardigan. His address was a credit not only to himself, his constituency and the Island, but indeed to Parliament itself.
It is a great honour for any member to sit in this chamber where sat also the great parliamentarians of modern Canadian history, men like Arthur Meighen, M. J. Coldwell, and Ernest Lapointe. It is a pleasure to be seated in this House, and much more a pleasure to be making a speech here for the first time. I am particularly delighted to be standing here in this Parliament as the successor to a distinguished Canadian, Dr. Heath Macquarrie, who represented Hillsborough with enormous distinction for over 22 years.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I acknowledge his presence in the House and am delighted both to succeed him and to see him here today. He made a most valuable contribution to Canadian affairs, to Hillsborough, to the Island, to Canada, and indeed to the world community through his interest and expertise, and his knowledge in the field of international affairs. I am glad that the Parliament of Canada will have the benefit of his formidable talents in the Upper Chamber, as a result of his appointment last week.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!
