speechtext:
The riding of Hillsborough of which I am the representative is essentially the greater Charlottetown area including West and East Royalty, Sherwood and Parkdale. It is not only the capital city area of Prince Edward Island, it is also the cradle of confederation itself. It is small geographically and by population, but its contribution to national affairs belies its very size and small population.
Hillsborough has a long and distinguished tradition of excellence in the field of higher education. It boasts a relatively new university, the University of Prince Edward Island, which was fathered by two established institutions, St. Dunstan's University and Prince of Wales College, which were older than Canada itself. Hillsborough has a first-rate community college for vocational and technical training, Holland College, and good primary and secondary schools. A special interest of mine is architecture and restoration and heritage, and my riding has some of the finest examples of early Canadian architecture to be found anywhere in the country.
I might mention also that the Confederation Centre of the Arts was built in 1964 as a result of taxpayers' contributions from every part of Canada, all ten provinces, the territories, and the dominion government. The Centre is now, and has been for some time, producing original Canadian musicals that are excellent by world standards.
[Mr. McMillan.)
We in the riding of Hillsborough, and in Prince Edward Island in general, enjoy perhaps a simpler life than Canadians in many other parts of the country. But it is a good life. It is a community where natural beauty, clean air and strong community ties are taken for granted. Our values are inherited largely from our Scottish, Irish, Acadian, and English ancestors. They have been enriched, however, by the contributions of people from all over the world who have given us the benefit of their cultures. My riding will be further enhanced by the arrival of some 500 new families from Ottawa following the relocation of the Department of Veterans Affairs.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Aren't you lucky?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We are, indeed, lucky. And I want to emphasize to those public servants who may feel some trepidation about having their families uprooted, that Islanders are looking forward to their arrival and are doing everything possible to make them feel welcome in their new community.
The whole business of the relocation of the Department of Veterans Affairs is a practical application of the principle of decentralization endorsed both by the previous government and by the current government. It is a principle which holds that the benefits to be derived from government itself as an industry should be spread as widely as possible across this great dominion. Mr. Speaker, it is not etched in stone that our national institutions or departments or agencies of government should, a priori, be ensconeed in the national capital area or in central Canada for that matter. I stress the importance of this relocation of the department to my riding. I think it is important, also, to the department, which I am sure, will be well accommodated in the city of Charlottetown. But to any public servants who may still have some reservations or hesitancy, some fears or anxieties about the reception they will find when they move to our community, I stress that those fears can be put to rest.
A moment ago I talked about educational opportunities in my riding-the fine university, an excellent community college, the first-class primary and secondary schools. I hope and anticipate and pray that by the expiry of this Parliament, whenever that may be, the city of Charlottetown will also be able to boast a first-class veterinary college. At present, we in Canada have only three veterinary schools, one in Guelph, one in Ste. Hyacinthe, and one in Saskatoon. There is none to serve the whole of Atlantic Canada. The only English-speaking veterinary school in eastern Canada, including Ontario, is in Guelph. And it is incapable of accepting more than six students from Atlantic Canada each year.
It is a fact that, each year in Canada, we are falling behind by some 100 trained veterinarians, the numbers required in the private and the public sectors alike. It is a tragedy, a national scandal, that we should be going outside our own country for trained veterinarians at the very time when our own qualified young people are being refused entrance to veterinary schools in Canada.
October 12, 1979

If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from a report prepared by Dr. R. G. Thomson, planning co-ordinator for the proposed Atlantic regional veterinary college.
In both agriculture and veterinary medicine there are acute shortages in Canada of professionally trained men and women for specialized posts in government and industry.
In certain fields the shortage is so critical that Government agencies are having to hire a significant proportion of their professional staff outside Canada. At present Agriculture Canada is sponsoring a number of professional employees in full-time studies at foreign graduate schools. While this may be commendable in terms of promoting Canadian participation in international scholarship, every Canadian should be embarrassed that we are relying on foreign schools to train a significant proportion of the country's highly qualified personnel in agriculture and veterinary medicine-two fields of education in which, given our natural and human resources, we should be providing world leadership rather than imposing upon others.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have for some time now, been a proponent of a fourth veterinary school for Canada. 1 would especially like it to be in my own riding. In any event, 1 certainly want it to be in Atlantic Canada because of our great regional need. As 1 go about making speeches, attending meetings, consultations and so on, I am sometimes asked whether Canada can afford another veterinary school. Sir, we cannot afford not to have one. The savings from improved animal care and from the prevention of animal and fish diseases would far exceed the cost of establishing a school. The Government of Canada under the previous administration committed itself to the establishment of a fourth veterinary school. The Maritime Provinces Higher Education Commission recommended that there be a fourth school in Canada and that it be not only in the Atlantic region but in Charlottetown, for good, sound academic reasons. Unfortunately, the project has now become bogged down because, I must say with regret, we maritimers have been arguing unduly among ourselves about the question of a site. Whether it is established in Truro, in Wolfville or in Charlottetown, 1 would urge the Council of Maritime Premiers, the forum in which a decision will have to be reached in the first instance, to put aside whatever parochial interests they may have for the good of the Atlantic region as a whole, and especially for the good of our young people.
1 have stressed the need to decrease our reliance on other countries for highly trained personnel. I have underlined the need for a veterinary school because it is a project which is dear to my heart and close to the interests of the Atlantic region. But the dire situation I have described with respect to our dependence on other countries for highly trained personnel is prevalent in a host of areas in higher education and in other aspects of our national life. The fact is we are graduating many hundreds of highly qualified Canadians, including Ph.Ds, who are unable to find suitable work or employment while, at the same time, we are going outside Canada to hire people who in many cases possess lesser qualifications. 1 am alarmed at the situation to be found in the universities in Canada especially in the light of their track record in hiring their own personnel. In case I may be misunderstood, misquoted, or quoted out of context, I want to stress that I am not suggesting that universities should propagandize for anything, or that they should proselytize for any cause. They are by
The Address-Mr. McMillan
definition international institutions and must not be circumscribed or restricted in any way by geographic or cultural factors.
But in Canada-and this is true of every country-we must have universities which address not only our international obligations but also our obligations to ourselves. Many Canadians believe strongly-and I share this view-that such a balance is somehow out of whack in their own country. Our Canadian universities have hired, and are continuing to hire, a greater proportion of non-nationals than are universities in any other country in the world.
If I may again quote a statistic or two, the ones I have are for the academic year 1976-1977, the year for which we have the most up-to-date figures-others will be forthcoming, and I am sure the picture will not be changed as a result of them- almost 30 per cent of our total university faculty was nonCanadian. That picture compares unfavourably with the situation in every other country. The corresponding figures for such great international universities as Harvard, Princeton, Yale, Oxford, Cambridge, the Sorbonne-any of them-hardly ever exceed 5 per cent, 6 per cent or 7 per cent.
In some disciplines in Canadian universities the situation is particularly dire. I regret that those are often the very fields in which our young people are most strongly motivated in their perception of themselves and of Canada as a whole. For example, in archaeology and anthropology, in 1976-77, almost half the faculty at Canadian universities was non-Canadian. In philosophy, almost 35 per cent of the faculty was non-Canadian; in geography, 35 per cent; in sociology, more than 35 per cent; in history, 30 per cent; in political science, 30 per cent; and on and on. Last year 35 per cent of new appointments at our universities went to non-Canadians. In the west the figure was 40 per cent, and if we exclude Quebec the picture was even worse nationally. I do not think I would be exaggerating if I said that this is a national scandal. It is a disgrace of which every concerned Canadian should be ashamed.
I realize that my time is limited here today, but I would like to mention two particularly harmful effects of the situation I have described. First, we are denying our own young people opportunities for positions in higher education, teaching positions, research positions and others. Second, and just as seriously, we are unduly exposing our young people's minds to teaching priorities and research interests which reflect other peoples' cultures.
I am not suggesting that we should erect a Great Wall of China around our country, around our universities or around our young people's minds. I am saying, though, that there is a significant neglect of Canadian studies because our faculties and our researchers are giving undue attention to priorities which they brought with them from other countries. Is it any wonder that we are graduating students, from every level of education, from primary and secondary levels through to community colleges, higher education, and universities, who

October 12, 1979
The Address-Mr. McMillan
lack a basic knowledge about the history, politics, sociology and science of their country?
If one wants to identify one of the root causes of our national unity problem, 1 think one need go no further.
I bring to the attention of hon. members an excellent report published by the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. This document was sponsored by them and written by Dr. T. H. B. Symons, chairman of the Commission on Canadian Studies. The report is called "To Know Ourselves" and it thoroughly documents the situation I have been able only to touch on. I highly recommend it as required reading for every concerned hon. member.
I recommend too the synopsis of that report for those who consider the size of it forbidding, a synopsis by the Book and Periodical Development Council of Canada, which is published as a public service by that council, and is readily available.
1 will conclude my remarks by expressing apology for any undue emphasis on the importance of higher education and research. But, with the indulgence of the House, 1 would like to mention one field in which I think there is a particular need for research and development, and that is the field of energy. As some will know, the province of Prince Edward Island is probably the most energy deficient piece of territory in all of Canada. We are 90 per cent dependent on conventional sources of energy, particularly oil, which is to say foreign oil. This has many implications for the cost of living and for our ability to cope with Canada's harsh winters. The implications are, however, particularly serious in terms of the haemorrhage of energy dollars from our region which this represents and, indeed, from our country.
1 want to say that every one in this House has a natural interest in the question of energy, the cost of living and attendant issues. But, I think we have to realize, as certainly the people in Prince Edward Island do, that we must do something about the high cost of energy and the ever escalating cost of that product. Too often we have been relying, I fear, on short-term measures and ad hockery. But, more seriously, perhaps, from the point of view of Prince Edward Island, the approach has too frequently been in the direction of global solutions, and this has been at the expense of looking at opportunities afforded by local situations, including climatic and geographic characteristics. I am not now going to enter into a debate as to whether nuclear energy is a good thing or a bad thing. I have no interest today in talking about the morality of that particular issue. I will address that question on another occasion as, I am sure, other members will.
Let me say, however, that the very heavy investment Canada has made in nuclear energy has practically elbowed off the stage altogether any attention to renewable energy sources. I am thinking in particular of the development of the technology of alternate energy. No one would suggest-and certainly I would not suggest today or at any other time-that alternate energy will ever replace totally, or even substantially in the foreseeable future, conventional sources of energy such as oil. But I do think it is possible to do a great deal more than

we are in directing research toward wind, solar heat, and wood-burning in particular.
In the province of Prince Edward Island, for example, it is often suggested that we are the million-acre farm. I think we are somewhat better endowed than that, for in our tiny piece of territory we have more than 600,000 acres of wood lots alone. This valuable resource could be cultivated, harvested and exploited, in the best sense of that word, for energy purposes now and for future generations.
I am not specially pleading, I hope, for Prince Edward Island, but I do suggest that our province constitutes an excellent potential laboratory for research and development in the renewable energy fields. As I already mentioned, we have an excellent university and other research facilities, some of them associated with government itself. There was created by a previous provincial government of a different political stripe from my own-I do not hesitate to give credit where credit is due-a superb Institute of Man and Resources devoted to the whole area of research and development in the renewable energy fields. That could constitute the nucleus for a first-class, impressive, massive investment by Canada, on a pilot project basis, in the renewable energy enterprise.
The fruits of such research would be particularly beneficial to the people of Prince Edward Island. Equally, I am convinced, the products and the benefits derived from such an enterprise could be shared by all Canadians. For example, I am thinking of the applicability of such research in northern Ontario, where conditions are very similar.
I should like to conclude on a positive note. I think all hon. members will join with me in suggesting that ours is an enormous challenge. Huge problems are facing our country, every province of Canada and every territory-in the energy field, in transportation, in regional development, in all aspects of the economy, in cultural affairs, and in many other fields. The challenges are formidable.
As the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) suggested earlier this week, ours is a new Parliament. Canadians have high expectations of this Parliament. They expect imaginative and courageous measures from us. We must not let them down.

Mr. Speaker, together with my colleagues I extend to you my best wishes for your reelection as Speaker of the House. I am confident the wisdom you have shown during the last parliament demonstrates beyond any doubt that the choice made by the House in nominating you will give to this Parliament the strength and the necessary power to operate in an equitable manner. Your task will certainly not be easy, Mr. Speaker, but I am convinced that you will show all the competence your position
October 12, 1979

requires and that this 31st parliament will be proud of its Speaker.
I would also like to congratulate the member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and his colleague the member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) for having sponsored the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne and I want to underline the remarkable manner in which they both have carried out this duty for it is not easy for a new member to take the floor for the first time in this House so filled with memories and where so many speeches have been delivered. I am convinced those two new colleagues, even though they are not on the right side, will be excellent members. Furthermore, 1 would like to congratulate the Prime Minister and all new cabinet members and assure them I will always be on their heels, not to be crushed, but rather to bite occasionally if Argenteuil were forgotten. For being elected I want to congratulate all those who like me are serving their first term in this Thirty-first Parliament. We joined battle in the last election, some fell and we, the newly elected, are proud of the mandate we were given by our respective people.
I would also like to extend my congratulations to all those who were re-elected, some not for the first time, and 1 under-
The Address-Mr. Gourd
stand the work they had to do because the work of a parliamentarian is to look after parliament's business in addition to an election period-it is not an easy thing. So I want to reiterate, Mr. Speaker, my congratulations to all those former re-elected members.
I would be remiss if I did not mention the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) who waged an excellent battle and who would also probably make a great Liberal. His team-and 1 remember my NDP opponent during the last campaign-stood for what we Liberals had put forward. That is why 1 had to congratulate the Leader of the New Democratic Party. But I would not want to forget a French-speaking colleague, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy), who is also sitting in this parliament for the first time. 1 am convinced he will be an asset to this House. We were able to see that yesterday when he showed us his oratorical talents. Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?
